en: The Profound Meaning of the *Sūtra on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma*, composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Gusu.
Now, the three realms are but mind; there is no dharma outside of mind. The principle-as-endowment and the phenomena-as-actualization are truly not two distinct layers. It is only due to delusion...
If one is deluded regarding them, the three obstructions appear vividly; if one awakens to them, the three virtues are their natural state (*dharmatā*).
Delusion and awakening have no inherent nature; they are provisional names established according to worldly convention. As for the true destination: they are two yet not-two, and not-two yet two.

Delusion and awakening seem to be distinct, yet since delusion is simply being deluded about that which is awakened to, awakening is simply awakening to that which was deluded about. This is the *Sūtra on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma*.

This is the essential ford for pointing out delusion and returning to awakening. "The practitioner" refers to the wisdom capable of contemplation; "the retribution of good and evil karma" refers to the objects of contemplation.
The subject of contemplation is none other than the one mind and its threefold wisdom; the object of contemplation is none other than the single realm and its threefold truth.
It eliminates doubts and hindrances, strengthens pure faith, reveals the expedient means for progress, and provides consolation.

It causes one to be free from timidity and weakness. Thus, the Great Sage Śākyamuni exhorted those for whom the teaching was intended to make a formal request, and the Compassionate Honored One Kṣitigarbha, impelled by his vow of compassion, expounded this teaching.
Both principle and phenomenon are clearly elucidated; both the shallow and the deep derive equal benefit.

It may truly be called a precious torch illuminating the dark alleys and a divine elixir curing chronic ailments. Although the time since the Sage departed is remote, how fortunate we are to encounter this wondrous [teaching].

The commentary remains extant. As my desire to study and revere it is so earnest, I cannot bring myself to desist. Drawing from the limited perspective of one measuring the ocean with a ladle or peering through a tube, I employ this work to align with your noble intent.

I shall now provide a sub-commentary on the scriptural text, beginning first by clarifying its profound meaning (*xuan-yi*). This consists of five sections: first, the explanation of names (*shi-ming*); second, the manifestation of the essence (*xian-ti*); third, the elucidation of the core tenet (*ming-zong*);
fourth, the discernment of its function (*bian-yong*); and fifth, the analysis of the doctrinal phases (*jiao-xiang*).

First, regarding the explanation of the title: the seven characters of the scripture’s title consist of six specific terms and one general term. Among the seven types of specific titles, this one follows the "single term based on the Dharma" (dharmapada).

The two characters "Occupying and Examining" (*zhànchá*) refer to the observing subject (the method), while the four characters "Wholesome and Unwholesome Karmic Retribution" (*shàn'è yèbào*) refer to the observed object (the phenomena).
In explaining these two—the subject and the object—there are again two sections: first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive explanation. This is the initial brief explanation.
"Zhan" (divination) takes "gazing" as its meaning; "cha" (examination) takes "thorough scrutiny" as its meaning. Each has its own principle:
regarding the "matter," one relies on the three types of wheel-signs shown by the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) and casts them with utmost sincerity—this is called "divination.
One then carefully observes whether they correspond or not—this is called "examination. Through these means, one either dispels one's own doubts or dispels the doubts of others.
One should simply study this Dharma and must not follow worldly methods of divination and astrology. As for "principle" (li):
it refers to being correctly directed toward reality, based upon the single true realm and the two types of contemplative paths shown by the Great Being; this is what is called "divination.
It relies on the profound Dharma skillfully taught by the Great Being, which is free from the fault of contradiction; one should examine it with earnest scrutiny.
This alone is called "examination. From this, one advances toward goodness oneself and causes others to also advance toward goodness;
one leaves behind timidity and weakness oneself and causes others to also leave behind timidity and weakness. This is called the "Examination of Principle.

As for good and evil, they consist of the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome paths of action, which are termed "karma" based on body, speech, and mind. Karma is simply volition (*cetanā*); it is through wholesome and unwholesome volition that [action] is initiated.

The various activities of body, speech, and mind—wherein the mind encompasses both afflictions and karma, while body and speech consist solely of karma—are now examined for the degree of their goodness or evil through the first wheel-sign, observing whether they are in accord with one another.
Furthermore, the strength or weakness of karmic power is examined through the second wheel-sign, which likewise requires observation of their mutual correspondence. Moreover, by means of the third...

Regarding the wheel-marks: one must observe and examine the karmic retributions of the three periods of time, and also investigate whether they correspond [to one's actions] or not, as extensively clarified in the sūtra text.
One should use these three types of wheel-marks to divinely examine the karmic retributions of all one’s own good and evil deeds, thereby resolving doubts and regrets;
the same applies when doing so for others. Therefore, it is called "Divining and Examining the Karmic Retributions of Good and Evil."
Furthermore, there are wholesome and unwholesome delusions, wholesome and unwholesome karmas, and the retributive fruits produced by wholesome and unwholesome karmas.

These three—delusion, karma, and fruit—are all produced by causes and conditions. Whatever belongs to the category of dharmas produced by causes and conditions is, without exception, identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Now, based on the single reality realm (*ekābhāsa-viṣaya*), to understand that which is identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is called "divination" (*zhan*). Furthermore...
Based on the two types of paths of contemplation, to realize that [all phenomena] are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is called *vicaya* (investigation).
Alternatively, based on the skillful means of progressive advancement, to know them as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, thereby instigating right faith, is called *vitarka* (reflection).

Furthermore, based on the skillful exposition of the profound Dharma, to awaken to their being emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, and thus forever abandon cowardice, is called *vicaya*. Therefore, it is so named.
This is the divination of the retribution of good and evil karma. The initial brief explanation is concluded.
Next, regarding the detailed explanation: following the convenience of the text, one should first explain "divination" (zhan-cha) and subsequently explain "the retribution of good and evil karma."
However, if there were no retribution for good and evil karma, on what basis could one discuss the practice of *zhancha* (divination/observation)?

Now, relying on this principle, I shall first explain the retribution of good and evil karma, and subsequently explain *zhancha*. The explanation of the retribution of good and evil karma is further divided into two parts.
First, the analysis of individual terms; second, the combined analysis. Within the first [section], there are three parts: first, the analysis of good and evil;

second, the analysis of karma; third, the analysis of retribution. Within the first [of these], the analysis of good and evil is divided into four parts: first, an analysis restricted to specific phenomena; second, an analysis according to universal principle;
third, the attribution of these to the ten dharma-realms; fourth, the conclusion that they are identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

First, regarding the explanation based on specific phenomena: that which is by nature pure and well-disciplined, capable of bringing benefit and advantage to this life and future lives, is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
That which is by nature defiled and coarse or unruly, capable of causing harm and disadvantage to this life and future lives, is [termed "unwholesome"].

These are called the unwholesome: namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; these are called the three unwholesome actions of the body. False speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech;
these are called the four unwholesome actions of the mouth. Covetousness, ill will, and delusion; these are called the three unwholesome actions of the mind.

Refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, and refraining from sexual misconduct; these are called the three wholesome actions of the body. Refraining from false speech, refraining from frivolous speech, refraining from divisive speech, and refraining from harsh speech.
The four virtues of speech are non-covetousness, non-anger, and non-delusion. The three virtues of mind are likewise [non-covetousness, non-anger, and non-delusion].

Thus, the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* states: "These ten matters do not accord with the Noble Path; they are called the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*). If these evils are ceased, they are simply called the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).

Furthermore, each of the ten wholesome actions is discussed in terms of both cessation (*saṃvara*) and practice (*caryā*). Refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, and so forth, are termed "cessation."
To practice kindness, compassion, and the release of living beings; to provide for all through charity; to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*); to speak words of truth;
to speak words that are beneficial and meaningful; to reconcile disputes; to instruct others with gentleness; to always maintain a mind of joy and renunciation;

and to dwell in a will of pity and sympathy while thoroughly understanding both phenomena and principles—this is called practicing goodness. Therefore, this sutra says: "That which is called the ten wholesome paths constitutes all [virtue]."
It is the root of all wholesome dharmas and is able to encompass all other wholesome dharmas.

As for what are called the ten unwholesome actions, they likewise constitute the root of all unwholesome dharmas and are able to encompass all other unwholesome dharmas. This concludes the initial explanation based on the specific categories of phenomena.
Second, regarding the comprehensive explanation based on principle (*li*), first the evil is explained, next the good is explained, and finally their mutual fusion is clarified.

First, regarding the explanation of evil: there is evil of phenomena (*dharma*) and evil of principle. Evil of phenomena is as previously described. Evil of principle refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who calculate [existence] in terms of annihilation or permanence, thereby destroying cause and effect;
this is the killing of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and a violation of *nirvāṇa*, whereby one cannot realize or accord with it. This is...
To kill the True Dharma; to hold views and the attachment to precepts and rituals as supreme; and to be attached to phenomena external to the mind—these are stealing.

To be stained by craving and dogmatic attachment, as well as to relish meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the like—these are sexual misconduct. To claim that what is not actually the path to liberation is the path to liberation—this is false speech.
Various frivolous discourses that lack true meaning—this is idle chatter. To cause strife and confusion regarding the supramundane Dharma—this is divisive speech. To increase... [the afflictions].

To harbor long-lasting afflictions and poisons is malicious speech (*pāruṣya*). To claim one’s own views are true while deeming others’ false is greed (*lobha*). Not knowing the means of deliverance is delusion (*moha*).
For *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, the permanent severing of the causes of birth is the killing of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Not knowing the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is the killing of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). Falsely grasping at *nirvāṇa* is theft (*steya*). To realize a partial truth and yet be unable to relinquish it is [the fault of] attachment.
To be detached from this lust yet not having attained all-encompassing liberation, while claiming to be liberated, is false speech. It is like an empty fist or a willow leaf;
it lacks any true reality and is thus frivolous speech. To separate the natures of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—which are non-dual—by establishing them as two distinct entities, is divisive speech.
To differentiate between dharmas such as good and evil, or the outflowing and the outflow-free, is [divisive speech].
Harsh speech; attachment to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is greed; aversion toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is anger; ignorance of the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is delusion.
When a Bodhisattva of expedient teaching enters emptiness, he "kills" the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); when he enters the provisional, he "kills" the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*);

when he contemplates the middle, he "kills" both truths simultaneously. To vow to attain *bodhi* [while still clinging to these stages] is theft; attachment to the Dharma through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) is lust; [this applies to one who has] not yet realized...
To have any verbal expression regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*) is false speech. Various expressions that do not accord with the true meaning are frivolous chatter.
To differentiate between the middle and the extremes is divisive speech. To revile and censure birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the teachings of the Two Vehicles is harsh speech.
Attachment to the Dharma that resembles the Path is greed (*rāga*). Abandoning the two extremes is hatred (*dveṣa*). Not yet illuminating the perfect middle is delusion (*moha*).

The explanation of evil is complete. Next, the explanation of good: mundane good is as previously described. As for ultimate good, the disciples of the Buddha depart from the views of annihilationism and eternalism and have deep faith in cause and effect;

this is non-killing according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). To realize that all phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, there is no inherent nature [in things]. Not killing is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

One knows that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the Ultimate Truth, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the abiding of the Dharma (*dharma-sthiti*), the fixed position of the Dharma (*dharma-vyavasthāna*), Suchness (*tathatā*), the Reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
These are equal, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable. Through the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*) of not killing, one realizes that there are no phenomena outside of the mind.

To take [only what is permissible] is non-stealing. To be without capacity and without object is non-lust. To explain according to principle through the four *siddhāntas* (the four types of truth) is non-falsehood.
To enable sentient beings to obtain the four benefits is non-frivolous speech. To accord with both phenomena and principle is [right action].
This is not causing strife; it gladdens the hearts of the multitude. This is not coarseness or malice; it is free from attachment to what merely resembles the Path.

This is not greed; it does not contradict the Three Truths. This is not anger; it thoroughly penetrates the Three Truths. This is not delusion. Having thus concluded the explanation of "good," the subsequent clarification of their mutual integration is as follows:
the names "good" and "evil" originally have no fixed definition; therefore, to define them by means of their names is impossible in ten thousand ways.
First, regarding the attainment [of names]: to establish names based on their meaning ensures that there is not one instance in ten thousand where an error occurs.
For example, if we consider them in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), then acts such as killing and stealing are evil, while refraining from killing and stealing are good.

If we consider them in terms of principle (*li*), then all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena—whether good or evil—are collectively termed "evil," whereas uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena and principles are termed "good. Furthermore, this includes contaminated good and evil, as well as the phenomena and principles of the limited truth (*pratisaṃvid*).

Taken collectively, these are termed "evil. When one enters into the provisional phenomena and their underlying principle, they are termed "good. Furthermore, regarding tainted good and evil, as well as the phenomena and principles of partial truth:

when one enters into the provisional phenomena and their underlying principle, they are collectively termed "evil"; when one enters into the phenomena and underlying principle of the Middle Way, they are termed "good."
Furthermore, the phenomena and principle of the "limited middle" (butian zhong) are still termed "evil," whereas the phenomena and principle of the "perfect middle" (yuanzhong) are termed "good.
Thus, phenomena such as killing and stealing can only be termed evil and cannot be termed good; the phenomena and principle of the perfect middle can only be termed good and cannot be termed evil.
This applies even to the non-killing and non-stealing of phenomena, up to and including the phenomena and principle of the limited middle.
They may be called "good," and they may also be called "evil. In relation to what precedes them, they are all called good; in relation to what follows them, they are all called evil.
Furthermore, there is "principle-evil" (*yili-aku*): namely, slaying the father Ignorance, harming the mother Craving, and taking Bodhi when none can give it.
Yet I take Bodhi for myself, with the Joy of Dharma as my wife, using the empty fist to entice and deliver beings, even unto great greed and great...
This Dharma-gate of great hatred and delusion is such that only the Buddha is fully possessed of the ten non-virtues;
Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles possess only a small portion of the ten non-virtues; and all sentient beings are able to possess only the ten virtues, without even a trace of evil.
Second, the general explanation based on principle is concluded.

Third, the summary regarding the affiliation with the ten dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) has three parts: first, clarifying the ten realms; second, clarifying the four teachings; and third, clarifying the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yukti*).
First, regarding the clarification of the ten realms: the realm of hell involves heavy suffering, yet it possesses both the seeds of phenomena and principle, as well as those of good and evil.
My son, they do not give rise to the actual manifestation of either virtuous or non-virtuous phenomena, whether on the level of events (*vṛtti*) or principles (*nyāya*).

The same applies to a portion of those in the realms of extreme suffering, such as hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*). These two realms of hungry ghosts and animals also possess both virtuous and non-virtuous seeds of both events and principles;

however, they frequently manifest non-virtuous events and rarely manifest virtuous events. They are not necessarily able to manifest non-virtuous or virtuous principles because their power of wisdom is weak. Asuras...

The realm of asuras is roughly similar to that of ghosts and animals. Should they happen to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, they are able to give rise to wholesome states of principle (*nyāya-kuśala*).
If such wholesome states of principle arise, they are accordingly subsumed within the four noble realms. The human realm is twofold:

those in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), although possessing all seeds, give rise only to wholesome actions of fact (*vastu-kuśala*) and do not give rise to unwholesome actions of fact; nor do they give rise to unwholesome states of principle or... [unwholesome states of principle].
Excellent. Regarding mundane goodness (*laukika-kuśala*), there are only the ten virtues of the old physicians;
they do not give rise to the goodness of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, or the Full Ordination, because they have not heard the Buddha-dharma.

If one is in [any of] the three continents, one is fully capable of giving rise to both mundane and supramundane (*lokottara*) good and evil, because the wisdom and understanding among humans are extremely sharp and keen. If one gives rise to supramundane goodness, it is also subsumed accordingly.
Within the four noble realms, there are four types of celestial destinies. First are the four earth-dwelling heavens, namely the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

these fully manifest both the phenomena and principles of good and evil, being roughly similar to humans, with the sole exception that within their virtuous activities they lack the single factor of monastic precepts.
Second are the four space-dwelling heavens, namely the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens; these do not give rise to killing or stealing.

Sexual misconduct consists of three kinds of unwholesome actions (*akuśala-karma-patha*). Although it remains, and correct sexual conduct has not yet been abandoned, it is still possible for the latter seven kinds of unwholesome actions to arise.

It is also capable of giving rise to the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*), though it does not give rise to the monastic precepts (*pravrajita-śīla*). Furthermore, it is also capable of giving rise to what is wholesome in principle (*tattva-kuśala*) and what is unwholesome in principle (*tattva-akuśala*).
If one gives rise to what is wholesome in principle, one is accordingly included within the four noble realms (*ārya-dhātu*): namely, the three realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and so forth. Moreover...

This is divided into two parts. First, in the heavens of the first dhyāna, there still exist vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and speech; thus, it is possible for verbal falsehood and mental covetousness to arise.

For instance, Brahmā gave rise to flattery and deception toward the Śākya son [the Buddha]. However, other forms of objective evil do not arise. One may give rise to all types of conceptual good or conceptual evil.
If one gives rise to conceptual good, it is also subsumed within the four noble realms. This applies from the second dhyāna upward as well.

Having already abandoned applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one does not give rise to physical or vocal actions that are unwholesome; rather, one gives rise only to the greed and delusion of that respective stage, as well as to wholesome or unwholesome states based on principle.

If one gives rise to wholesome states based on principle, these belong to the four noble realms. In the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there are only the four aggregates (*skandha*) and no body produced by karmic fruit;
thus, one does not give rise to physical or vocal actions that are wholesome or unwholesome, nor does one give rise to the greed and delusion of that respective stage.
Unwholesome states arising from reasoning are numerous, while those arising from wholesome reasoning are few; this is because no Bodhisattvas give rise to them.

Furthermore, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are divided into three categories: first, those on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); second, those who have abandoned desire (*vītarāga*); and third, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

In the initial stage of the Path of Seeing, one eternally severs ten kinds of conceptualized unwholesomeness, as well as the killing of worldly beings and the killing of the Real (*satya*) by non-Buddhists, and so forth.

They possess the conceptual fault (*dṛṣṭi-doṣa*) of [viewing] misconduct as evil, yet they have not yet severed the actual misconduct of sexual misconduct, nor the spontaneous faults of greed, hatred, and delusion;

furthermore, they fully give rise to the conceptual faults of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. In the two stages of freedom from desire, they permanently sever the ten kinds of actual misconduct belonging to the Desire Realm.
The evil of spontaneous greed and delusion regarding the realms of form and formlessness has not yet been severed. The three stages of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are further divided into two:

first, the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), which permanently severs the evil of phenomena (*vastu-dauṣṭulya*) across the three realms and completely eliminates the evil of principle (*tattva-dauṣṭulya*) pertaining to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
second, the stage without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*). According to the provisional teachings, this is the permanent entry into *nirvāṇa*, wherein there is no longer any [evil of] phenomena.
Regarding the principles of good and evil, whether manifest or as seeds: if one discusses them according to reality, these pertain to the skillful means lands outside the birth-realm (*dhātu*).
One merely severs the manifest and seeded good and evil of both phenomena and principle within the realm;

yet, one may still manifest the irrational evil of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, or be able to give rise to the rational good and irrational evil of the Bodhisattva and Buddha realms. If one gives rise to [the latter],...
The good and evil of the Buddha-realm are to be subsumed accordingly within the Bodhisattva-Buddha realm. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu is divided into four [categories].
First, there are the Bodhisattvas of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as elucidated in the Tripiṭaka;

they possess the seeds of both good and evil regarding phenomena and principle, yet their power of great vows is strong while their power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is weak. Consequently, they are only able to permanently sever the active manifestation of phenomenal evil, but not...
They are able to cultivate the seeds of evil that cause harm, yet they can only ardently practice what is conventionally good;
they are unable to skillfully initiate what is good in principle. Since the original teaching does not establish stages of cultivation and realization, to speak of them in terms of actual reality:

They still belong merely to the realms of humans and devas. Second, the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): if they are at the stage of Dry Wisdom (Ganhui), they are roughly the same as those of the Tripitaka;

if they have realized the truth at the stage of the Eight Persons (Baren) or the Path of Seeing (Jian-di), they permanently sever the two kinds of evil—both phenomenal and noumenal—of ordinary beings, and are able to give rise to the phenomenal goodness and noumenal goodness of the Bodhisattva and Buddha realms. Third, the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) at the stage of the Ten Faiths (Shixin).

The intermediate [stage] is also the same as the Tripiṭaka. From the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onward, it is the same as the aforementioned Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), or perhaps even superior to it; this can be understood through reflection.

Upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), the realization of the Way is identical to the Perfect [Teaching]. One eternally severs the two kinds of evil—phenomenal and noumenal—of the nine realms, giving rise only to the two kinds of goodness—phenomenal and noumenal—of the Buddha-realm, as well as the noumenal evil of the Buddha. The Bodhisattvas of the fourth, the Perfect Teaching, are also called Bodhisattvas. They are also...

One is called a Buddha. Within the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-vastu*), one completely subdues the two types of evil—phenomenal and noumenal—of the nine realms, and completely gives rise to the phenomenal goodness of the Buddha-realm;

yet, the noumenal goodness and noumenal evil of the Buddha-realm have not yet manifested. Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one spontaneously first severs the two types of evil—phenomenal and noumenal—of ordinary beings in the external world, and also severs the noumenal evil of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, giving rise to a semblance [of the Buddha-realm].

Regarding the principle of good and the principle of evil within the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*): from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward, one completely severs the two evils—of both fact and principle—pertaining to the nine realms, and partially realizes the two principles of good and evil within the Buddha-realm. The Buddha-realm also has four aspects:

first, the resultant Buddha as elucidated in the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings, who is able only to permanently sever the seeds of the two evils of fact and principle pertaining to the six ordinary realms, thereby perfecting the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) facts and principles.
Second, regarding the two types of goodness: Cessation (*śamatha*) is able to slay the father of ignorance—the branches and leaves—and destroy the mother of craving within the realms.
It takes up the Bodhi of All-Knowledge and makes the joy of the Dharma of True Reality its wife. It uses the unspeakable Dharma that is beyond birth and death to entice the infant.
It does not abandon the conditioned merit and wisdom of the triple world as a great craving, yet it does not grasp at the views and afflictions of the triple world.

Grasping at cause and effect constitutes great hatred; failing to discern the various phenomena of the three realms constitutes great delusion. Regarding the Buddha of the fruit as elucidated in the second, the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna):

although the causal stage has already severed the seeds of the six mundane matters and the two types of evil—both phenomenal and noumenal—when the time of the fulfillment of the fruit arrives, it is still identical to the Buddha of the Hīnayāna (Zàngfó).
It differs only in that [the latter] can additionally preach the Dharma of the unarisen and the ineffable.

To entice an infant [with such things] is merely a minor victory. Third, the fruit-Buddha of wondrous enlightenment as elucidated in the Separate Teaching (Pṛthag-naya) has only severed twelve grades of the evil of ignorance;
it has only partially realized the two virtues of principle and phenomena within perfect centrality;

and it has only partially realized the cessation of great greed, great anger, and other evils. It cannot be called ultimate. Fourth, the fruit-Buddha of wondrous enlightenment as elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna).
All dualities of phenomena and principle—both evil and good—are severed without exception and cultivated to full completion.
Furthermore, one ultimately slays the father of ignorance and ultimately destroys the mother of craving; one ultimately attains great bodhi without remainder.
One ultimately unites with the joy of the Dharma of the Three Truths, never abandoning it for even a moment, life after life.

These four propositions are all inexpressible, yet they are spoken as: "all is real," "all is unreal," "all is both real and unreal," and "all is neither real nor unreal. These are taught to delude and entice the infants of the ten realms.
Not abandoning any phenomena, not grasping at any phenomena, and not discriminating any phenomena—this is called ultimate goodness and ultimate evil.
This concludes the initial explanation of the ten realms.

Second, regarding the explanation of the four teachings: each of the four teachings discusses the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), yet they differ in their relative shallowness or depth, and in their commonality or distinctiveness.

Now, we shall proceed by clarifying the profound based on the shallow, and subsuming the common under the distinct. For instance, in the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) Teaching, the objects to be remedied are the two evils of external phenomena and internal principles;
the remedies are the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections of the Three Vehicles. As for ordinary beings...
Externally, there are these six realms: the realm of the śrāvakas is the Four Noble Truths; the realm of the pratyekabuddhas is the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
the realm of the bodhisattvas is the Six Perfections; and the realm of the buddhas is the attainment of perfect enlightenment through the fulfillment of the causes over three great aeons.

Yet, when one investigates that which is expressed by these, it ultimately culminates in the single phrase: "dharmas arise through dependent origination. By analyzing phenomena until they return to emptiness, one severs the notion of self.

[The text] maintains that [these practitioners] do not realize that the essence of all phenomena is itself emptiness; rather, for the sake of transforming those of dull faculties, these minor teachings are bestowed.

If categorized according to the Bodhisattva path, they do not transcend the six classes of ordinary beings; if categorized according to their realization of truth, they merely revert to the extinction of ashes (nirvāṇa with remainder).

Restricting the general to the specific, this is judged to be the Dharma of the Śrāvaka. Next, the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna) is explained; it likewise takes the two evils of external phenomena and principles as its object.
As for the remedy, the contemplation of the principle of non-arising through shared *prajñā* serves as the antidote. The "ordinary" and "external" refer to the six dharma-realms (*ṣaḍ-dharmadhātu*).

The "ground of those who have completed their task" refers to the realm of the śrāvakas; the "ground of the pratyekabuddhas" refers to the realm of the pratyekabuddhas; the ninth ground is the realm of the bodhisattvas; and the tenth ground is the realm of the Buddhas.
Yet, when one investigates that which is signified, it ultimately consists of the single phrase "identical with emptiness. This is its essence.
The Dharma is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). It severs the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) within the realm of cessation.

Although it does not realize that all dharmas are merely provisional names and are immeasurable, and though it serves as the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, its teaching ultimately returns to the extinction of ashes (*bhasma-uccheda*). Restricting the general to the particular, this is judged to be the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Next, the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*) is clarified: it takes the two evils of the nine realms—both phenomenal and noumenal—as the objects to be remedied, by means of the "unshared" [wisdom].

The three successive contemplations of the *Prajñāpāramitā* serve as the remedies. Within the stage of the Ten Faiths, one looks up to faith in the Middle Way, employing the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*vibhaṅga-śūnyatā*) and the phenomenal goodness of the six perfections from the *Āgama* teachings to remedy the two evils of phenomena and principle regarding external ordinary beings.

In the Ten Abidings, one employs the contemplation of the essence of emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*) and the principled goodness of the six perfections from the *Vaipulya* teachings to sever the two evils of phenomena and principle regarding external ordinary beings. In the Ten Practices...

By employing the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-darśana*), one remedies the intellectual afflictions of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; one is able to universally penetrate the diseases and medicines of the ten realms.

In the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), one practices the contemplation of the Middle Way to remedy the intellectual afflictions of the Bodhisattvas. In the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), one severs the intellectual afflictions of the nine realms and realizes the intellectual goodness of the Buddha-realm.
Yet, upon investigating that which is expressed, it is ultimately nothing more than the single phrase "provisional name" (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*), which takes principle as its object.
It cuts off nine [stages]. It does not realize that the very substance of all dharmas is itself the Middle Way.

Although it is said that the realization of the Way is identical to the Perfect [Teaching], when the principles discussed in its specific teaching are not yet fully integrated, it restricts the general to the particular and judges this to be the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. Next, the Perfect Teaching is explained:

the two evils of the ten realms, both in terms of phenomena and principle, are taken as the objects to be remedied; the two goods of the ten realms, both in terms of phenomena and principle, are taken as the remedies.
It may also be said that the principle of the ten realms' goodness is the object to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*), while the principle of the ten realms' evil is the remedy (*pratipakṣa*).
It may also be said that both the good and evil of the ten realms are the objects to be remedied, and both the good and evil of the ten realms are themselves the remedy.

Why is this? When the three thousand [realms] abide in principle, they are all equally termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Outside of the nature that acts as the remedy, there is no separate object to be remedied; it is like water forming ice.
When the three thousand fruits are realized, they are all called "permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Because the natures of the objects to be remedied have changed, there is no external remedy;
it is like ice returning to become water. Although there is neither subject nor object, yet subject and object appear distinct, because of this single [principle].
The three contemplations of the mind (*citta-trividha-vipaśyanā*) perfectly remedy all evils of phenomena and principles, and perfectly manifest all virtues and evils of principles.

From the five stages of the *pañca-vidyā* up to the stage of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, that which is severed and that which is manifested are briefly as previously described. However, to investigate their ultimate purport:
it clarifies that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; that causes and conditions are themselves the Middle Way; and that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are [identical].

There is no distinction. He preaches the dharma of non-discrimination, speaking according to the Buddha’s own intention. By grouping the general together with the specific, it is judged to be the dharma of the Buddha-realm.
This concludes the explanation of the four teachings.

Regarding the "Three Clarities and Six Stages of Realization": since the Perfect Teaching clarifies that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas and that their inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are equal, failure to understand this may easily give rise to arrogance and presumption.
Therefore, one must employ the six stages to distinguish the process of cultivation. Although cultivation is divided into six stages, the nature remains eternally equal;

thus, while there are six stages, they are always identical [to the ultimate]. This can dispel both discouragement and fear. Although the nature is equal, cultivation may be either regressive or progressive.

Therefore, they are identical yet always six; this can eliminate overweening pride (*adhimāna*). In principle, they are only "contrary" (*pratīpa*); in their ultimate realization, they are only "concordant" (*anuloma*).
From the stage of "name" (*nāman*) onward, looking back toward what precedes, they are called "concordant"; looking forward toward what follows, they are called "contrary.

Furthermore, the nature of contrariness is concordance with ignorance (*avidyā*), while the nature of concordance is contrariety to ignorance. Thus, contrariness may be termed "evil," yet it may also be termed "good"; concordance is termed "good," yet it is also... [the same].

This may be called "evil. As for the initial principle of "immediate identity" (*jiri-ji*), consider, for example, the single character for "good" (*zen*): it inherently encompasses the ten realms of existence.

Because one follows the father of ignorance (*mumyō*) and serves the mother of craving (*tōai*), one does not dare to steal the Bodhi; one remains estranged from the wife and concubines of Dharma-joy; one does not engage in verbal karma regarding the Buddha-dharma;
one does not covet the two kinds of goodness—of phenomena and principle; and one does not harbor anger toward the afflictions of views and thought.
If one clearly gives rise to delusions and creates karma through affliction, this constitutes the dharma-realm of the three miserable realms (trāya).

Conversely, if one does not kill even within the Middle Truth, does not grasp at one's own mind, does not cling to what resembles craving, does not preach teachings of provisional meaning, does not covet expedient virtues, and does not harbor anger toward the two extremes, thereby thoroughly comprehending the Three Truths, this constitutes the Buddha-realm. Furthermore, even when raising a single character for "evil," it likewise possesses [all these qualities].
Regarding the ten realms: by the fulfillment of the ten non-virtues, such as killing and stealing, one falls into the dharma-realm of the three miserable states.
By the fact that although one does not engage in actual evil deeds, one possesses the evil of delusion regarding ultimate truth, one falls into the dharma-realm of humans and devas.

Although there is no evil of phenomena nor evil of delusion regarding the ultimate truth, there is evil of delusion regarding conventional reality; thus, one falls into the Dharma-realm of the Two Vehicles.
Although there is no evil of phenomena, nor evil of delusion regarding the ultimate or conventional truths, there is evil of delusion regarding the middle truth;

thus, one falls into the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattvas. Although there is no evil of phenomena or evil of delusion regarding the Three Truths, one fully possesses the [karmic retribution for] killing ignorance.
If one commits evil such as patricide, one falls into the Buddha-realm. Thus we know that the two names, "good" and "evil," each possess the ten realms.

Within each individual realm, there is nothing that is not itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Yet the six classes of ordinary beings are like those born blind, unaware of this in their daily lives;

the followers of the Two Vehicles are like those with impaired vision, falsely giving rise to grasping and rejecting; and Bodhisattvas regard them as being beyond the screen, as if they were outside the barrier. Therefore, from the hells up to...
Distinct from the ten transferences, though one dwells in principle all day long, one does not attain the application of that principle; this is all termed "Buddha as Principle" (*li-ji*).
It is also termed "the ten realms as Principle," and it is also termed "good and evil as Principle. Second, regarding "Name-as-Such" (*ming-zi-ji*):
if one hears the wondrous exposition of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], one can understand that all good and evil exist merely as names, and that all ten realms likewise exist merely as names.
Names. Each and every name is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Within a single name, one penetrates all names;
all names penetrate back into a single name. It is neither one nor many, yet it is both many and one.
Therefore, names are themselves the Buddha; names are themselves the ten realms; and names are themselves [the Dharma].

This refers precisely to good and evil. Regarding the "identity of the three contemplative practices": based on the meaning one has understood, one gives rise to correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and carefully contemplates the good and evil within the ten realms.
One realizes that each and every thing is none other than the secret treasury of the three virtues. Consequently, one is able to perfectly subdue the five stages of delusion;
though afflictions exist, they are as if non-existent, and though one possesses only the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye.

This is the stage of contemplative practice as Buddhahood (*kuan-hsing-chieh fo*). It is also called the ten realms as contemplative practice (*kuan-hsing-chieh shih-chieh*). Contemplative practice as such consists of both good and evil.

Regarding the four stages of semblance (*si hsiang-si-chieh*): through the power of perfect contemplation (*yuan-kuan*), one eliminates the evils of both phenomena and principle (*shi-li*) and gives rise to the goodness of both phenomena and principle.
It is like drilling wood for fire, where the sign of warmth appears first; or like melting solid ice, which gradually causes it to become moist.
Therefore, it is called "similarity-identity" (sōji-soku) with the Buddha, and also called "similarity-identity" of the ten realms. It is also the "similarity-identity" of good and evil.

Regarding "partial realization-identity" (bunbun-shō-soku), through the power of perfect contemplation (*enkan*), one partially breaks through the three delusions above [the desire realm] within the good and evil of the ten realms, and partially manifests the ten [realms].

Regarding the three virtues of the superior [stages] within the realms of good and evil: they are like fire produced from wood that returns to burn the wood itself, or like ice becoming water that returns to melt the remaining ice;
therefore, they are called "partial realization as Buddha," also called "partial realization as the ten realms," and also called "partial realization as good and evil.
Sixth, "ultimate realization" refers to the fulfillment of the perfect path, wherein no delusions remain unbroken.
There is no virtue that is not manifested. It is like fire emerging from wood until the wood is exhausted, or like ice melting away until the water is clear.

Therefore, it is called "ultimate identity with the Buddha" and also "ultimate identity with the ten realms. It is "ultimate identity with good and evil," because the principle of the three truths and three virtues is inherently present within the good and evil of the ten realms, and only upon reaching this stage does it fully manifest. There is no separate dharma apart from this.
It can be realized and attained; it is simply the realization and attainment of the fundamental principle that sentient beings are deluded about. Therefore, it is said:
"Perfect Bodhi returns to non-attainment. This concludes the third section on the threefold synthesis belonging to the ten dharma-realms.
Fourth, the conclusion regarding the identity of the three—emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way:

All that has been clarified above concerning phenomena and principle, good and evil, encompasses the ten realms, universally subsumes the four teachings, and comprehensively includes the six stages of realization.

Thus, whether it be principle or phenomenon, cause or fruit, the signifier or the signified, or innate nature versus cultivated practice, medicine versus disease—all are fully contained within the two characters "good" and "evil. Therefore:
If one knows that good and evil are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle, then one knows that all dharmas are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle.
This perfectly integrated and wondrous principle is transparently clear at every point. Furthermore, there are three points of meaning: first, a vertical synthesis; second, a horizontal synthesis;
and third, a synthesis of a single thought-moment as being neither horizontal nor vertical. Regarding the first, the vertical synthesis: this refers to the goodness of phenomena (*dharma*).

There are two types of evil: evil in terms of phenomena (*vastu*) and evil in terms of principle (*tattva*). These belong to the dharma-realm of the six classes of ordinary beings and are that which is to be remedied by the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings.

That which falls within the stage of the position of principle is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), namely, "dharmas produced by causes and conditions. There are also two types of goodness:

goodness in terms of uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-vastu*) and goodness in terms of the realization of true principle. These belong to the dharma-realm of the Two Vehicles and pertain to the remedial dharma-gates of both the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings.

If distinguished, it is the "Identity of Principle" (*li-ji*) of the Perfect Teaching; if subsumed, it is identical to the "Similar Identity" (*xiang-si-ji*) of the Perfect Teaching—this is termed the "True Truth.

That which is called "I say it is precisely emptiness" refers to this. Entering into the two excellences of phenomena and principle in the provisional realm belongs to the *dharmadhātu* of the Bodhisattva.

From the perspective of the Path of Teaching in the Distinct Teaching (*bie-jiao*), if distinguished, it is also the "Identity of Principle"; if subsumed, it is likewise identical to the [Similar Identity].
"Resemblance" refers to the mundane and supramundane conventional truths that are like illusions; it is also termed "provisional designation.

It encompasses both the excellence of phenomena and principle within the Middle Way, as well as the faults of the Middle Way's principles, all of which belong to the Buddha-dharma realm. This is explained according to the perfect expression of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
That which begins from names and concludes with the ultimate is called the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth); it is also termed the meaning of the Middle Way.
Second, regarding the horizontal connection: this refers to the phenomena and principles, as well as the good and evil, of the ten realms as elucidated by the four teachings.
There is not a single thing that is not a phenomenon born of causes and conditions. There is not a single thing that is not itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Why is this so?
It is because within the single nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are naturally and inherently present the seeds of all phenomena—both good and evil—belonging to the ten realms;

these are called "causes. Depending upon conditions such as delusion or enlightenment, defilement or purity, they give rise to the various distinctions among the good and evil phenomena of the ten realms.

It is distinct. Since these ten realms, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are all produced through causes and conditions, they are definitively devoid of intrinsic nature when examined by means of the fourfold negation—neither self-produced, nor other-produced, nor both, nor without cause.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; being empty, this absence of intrinsic nature does not obstruct their arising through conditions.
One is all; they mutually encompass and mutually contain one another. Therefore, it is called "provisional" (*prajñapti*).

Being devoid of intrinsic nature yet arising through conditions, and arising through conditions while being devoid of intrinsic nature, every phenomenon (*dharma*) is without exception the totality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Outside of this dharma-nature, there is no other entity whatsoever.

All distinctions between internal and external, emptiness and existence, are extinguished. Therefore, it is called "middle" (*madhyama*). Third, regarding a single thought-moment, it is neither horizontal nor vertical.

To summarize: previously, we discussed vertical integration, wherein the Three Truths are respectively assigned to the ten realms. Next, we discussed horizontal integration, wherein each of the ten realms possesses its own Three Truths.
Vertically, they are distinct; horizontally, they are concurrent. How can this concurrency and distinction, this horizontality and verticality, manifest the ultimate principle?
Now we clarify that one should distinguish good and evil solely based on the single thought-moment of the present, relying exclusively upon this one thought-moment.

The ten realms are distinguished according to phenomena and principle, as well as good and evil; it is based solely upon these ten realms that the Four Teachings are elucidated, and it is based solely upon the Four Teachings that the Six Identities are discerned.
Within a single thought-moment, the principle is without before or after—how then can it be called "vertical" or "distinct"?

Within a single thought-moment, the essence is without this or that—how then can it be called "horizontal" or "simultaneous"? The essence of the thought-moment transcends all dependence; it is forcibly designated as "the Middle. One.
The center is the center of all things. Whether horizontal or vertical, there is nothing that is not immediately the center.

The essence of the center is free from all marks; it is forcibly termed "emptiness. When one thing is empty, all things are empty. Whether horizontal or vertical, there is nothing that is not immediately empty.

The essence of the center possesses all phenomena; it is forcibly termed "provisional. When one thing is provisional, all things are provisional. Whether horizontal or vertical, [there is nothing that is not immediately provisional].
There is nothing that is not immediately provisional. A sutra states: "The essence of the sentient beings' mind has been, from the very beginning, neither arising nor ceasing;
it is intrinsically pure, unobstructed, and without hindrance, just like empty space, because it is free from discrimination. This clarifies that a single thought-moment is itself the Middle Way.
It further states: "It is equal and pervasive, reaching everywhere; it is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions..."
Ultimately, it is a single characteristic; it is without duality or distinction, without change or difference, and without increase or decrease.

This clarifies that the mind of a single thought-moment is itself emptiness. Furthermore, it says: "The minds of all sentient beings, the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the minds of all bodhisattvas, and the minds of all buddhas are all identical in being neither arising nor ceasing, and are without defilement."
It is quiescent, because it is the characteristic of true suchness (*tathatā*). This clarifies that the single thought-moment is itself provisional. Furthermore, it says:
"If there were no conscious awareness capable of discernment, then there would be no differentiated characteristics of all objects throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time."
This clarifies that "when one is empty, all are empty. It further states: "Because all phenomena cannot exist of themselves, but exist only through the conceptual discrimination of the deluded mind;
this clarifies that 'when one is provisional, all are provisional. It further states:
"One should know that all dharmas are collectively termed 'mind,' because their essential nature is not different [from the mind] and they are subsumed within the mind."

This clarifies that within one there is all. Therefore, if one can thoroughly comprehend the mental phenomena of the single thought-moment of the present, then one will be able to universally penetrate the ten realms of good and evil, the four teachings, and the six stages of realization—all of which are neither horizontal nor vertical.

Furthermore, one will be able to universally illumine the ten realms of good and evil, the four teachings, and the six stages of realization, whether they be horizontal or vertical; this can be known through the mind. Is it not so?

This concludes the explanation of good and evil. Second, the explanation of karma (*karman*) is also divided into four parts: first, the explanation of its meaning; second, the classification of its types; third, the correlation with the ten dharma-realms;

and fourth, the conclusion that it is identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. First, regarding the explanation of its meaning: the term "karma" refers to "action" (*kriyā*), and it is also called "that which is produced. Furthermore—

It is called "movement" (*īryā*) and is also termed "constructing" (*saṃskāra*). According to the Hīnayāna, it exists only on the level of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and does not receive the name "karma.

Only when it moves the body and initiates speech is it designated as karma. According to the Mahāyāna, however, the momentary stirring of a single thought-impulse already constitutes the intention of karma.
As a sutra says: "Throughout day and night, sentient beings, in every moment of thought, produce various kinds of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)."
This refers to the world of sentient beings, the world of the physical realm, and the world of conventional designations.
Second, regarding the classification of types: first, unwholesome karma; second, wholesome karma. Furthermore, first, contaminated karma; second, uncontaminated karma.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of discrimination: first, contaminated karma; second, uncontaminated karma; third, karma that is both contaminated and uncontaminated;

and fourth, karma that is neither contaminated nor uncontaminated. First, unwholesome karma refers to the karma of the five heinous crimes, the ten unwholesome paths of action, stinginess, envy, violation of precepts, distraction, evil wisdom, and various false views. Second, wholesome karma refers to the karma of giving and ethical discipline.

There are karmas of meditative concentration and wisdom, as well as contaminated (sāsrava) karmas. Contaminated karma refers to the ten unwholesome actions that can bring about the retribution of non-merit;

the ten wholesome actions that can bring about the retribution of merit and happiness; and the four dhyānas and four concentrations that can bring about the retribution of the imperturbable (āniñjya).
Uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma refers to the noble paths cultivated by supramundane sages, which do not induce the ripening retribution of the three realms; it is solely...

One realizes the sublime fruit of purity and liberation. Furthermore, there are two types of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena: first, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) untainted phenomena, which is the suchness (*tathatā*) realized;
this is not termed "karma. Second, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) untainted phenomena, which is the merit and wisdom that realize [suchness].
Merit is called the auxiliary path; wisdom is called the true path. Both merit and wisdom are termed "karma. Regarding the fourfold distinction:
the wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable karmas of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

The karma of the two vehicles for transcending birth and death is termed "without outflows" (*anāsrava*). The karma of Bodhisattvas for delivering sentient beings, which does not grasp at *nirvāṇa*, is likewise [termed without outflows].

It is with outflows (*sāsrava*). Yet, because it does not defile birth and death, it is also called "without outflows" (*anāsrava*). These are the wondrous activities of the Buddhas that accord with their true nature (*dharmatā*);

they are not "with outflows," as they differ from those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), nor are they "without outflows," as they differ from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Alternatively, they are activities corresponding to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Karma associated with the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya) is called "with outflows" (sāsrava). Karma associated with the Middle Truth (madhyama-satya) is called "without outflows" (anāsrava).

When characterized by the simultaneous negation [of both extremes], it is called "neither with nor without outflows"; when characterized by the simultaneous illumination [of both], it is called "both with and without outflows. Regarding the inclusion of the four within the two: [it is as follows].

If one follows the doctrinal intent regarding the internal realms (*dhātu*), then the contaminated (*sāsrava*) includes only the contaminated, while the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fully includes the latter three.
If one follows the doctrinal intent regarding the external realms, then the contaminated fully includes the first three, while the uncontaminated includes only the fourth.

If one speaks according to the intention of connecting the specific [categories], then the "leaked" (sāsrava) and the "both" categories are collectively termed "leaked," while the "unleaked" (anāsrava) and the "neither" categories are collectively termed "unleaked.
Furthermore, if one applies the mutual inclusion of the wholesome and the unwholesome: either the ten unwholesome paths are taken as unwholesome and the ten wholesome paths as wholesome;
or else, that which is distracted is all unwholesome, while that which is concentrated is wholesome—or, alternatively, it is the leaked.
All [conditioned phenomena] are evil; the untainted (*anāsrava*) is good. Or, both the tainted and the untainted are evil; illuminating both simultaneously is good.
Or, even while illuminating both, it is still called evil; the simultaneous negation (*ubhaya-pratiṣedha*) that merges them into the same true reality (*dharmatā*) is good.

Or, the simultaneous negation that they are not identical to all phenomena is evil; the simultaneous illumination that there is nothing that is not the true reality is good. Or, everything is called evil. One—
All of these are termed "wholesome," as fully explained in the preceding text. Furthermore, these various wholesome and unwholesome karmas are broadly divided into four categories:

first, those to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*); second, those to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*); third, those to be experienced in subsequent births (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*); and fourth, those of indefinite timing (*aniyatavedanīya*).

This distinction arises due to the strength or weakness of the mind at the time of action, the high or low status of the object, and whether the karma has been moistened or not, or whether it has been confessed.

Because they have not yet been repented and are of various different kinds, they constitute four distinct categories. Second, the classification of types is concluded. Third, regarding the attribution to the ten dharma-realms, there are also three parts: first, explaining the ten realms; second, explaining the four teachings; and third, explaining the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yukti*).
