first, explaining the ten realms; second, explaining the four teachings; and third, explaining the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yukti*). First, explaining the ten realms: regardless of whether they are called good or evil, or tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), they are as follows:
Even regarding karma that is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, if one, in every thought-moment, clings to the notions of self and person,
devotes oneself solely to fame and profit, benefits oneself while harming others, and fails to reflect upon the consequences; if one’s actions of body, speech,

and mind follow exclusively the habit-energy of delusion, lacks faith in the Triple Gem, violates the precepts of ritual conduct, errs regarding cause and effect, and kills those who are worthy of respect— this is called hell.
The paths of karma are categorized as the ten grave evils of the superior grade.

If, in every moment of thought, one clings to the notions of self and person, indulges freely in sensual desires, lacks shame and remorse, is blind and ignorant, mired in the darkness of folly, and harbors many enmities and fetters—this is called the path of karma of animals, categorized as the ten evils of the middling grade. If, in every moment of thought, one clings to the notion of self...
A person who is stingy, greedy, and envious, who does not know how to plant roots of merit but only accumulates the seeds of transgression—this is called the karmic path of hungry ghosts.

These are categorized as the lower grade of the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*). Furthermore, if in every moment of thought one harbors a mind of flattery and deception, lacking any sense of integrity or straightforwardness.

To outwardly practice benevolence and righteousness while inwardly harboring notions of self and personhood, performing various deeds with a mind intent on victory or defeat—this is called the karmic path of the asuras.

It is categorized as the lower grade of the ten wholesome paths of action. If, in every thought-moment, one fears falling into suffering, restrains the five desires, maintains the mind in the precepts, and seeks future existence—this is called the karmic path of humans. It is categorized as [the middle grade].

The middling grade of the ten wholesome paths of action consists of, in every moment of thought, wishing that one may constantly experience superior bliss in the future, extensively performing various merits, and restraining all transgressions, even up to gathering the distracted mind into dhyāna and reviling form to enter emptiness; these are called the karmic paths of the celestial realm.
When these are consolidated as the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action, it consists of, in every moment of thought, observing the suffering of the three realms.

Emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness and with deep faith in dependent origination, one forever severs the mind that seeks future existence and directs its will solely toward the bliss of quiescent unconditioned nirvana.
This is called the path of action of the two vehicles, which is subsumed as the ten wholesome paths of superior grade, untainted by outflows (*anāsrava*).
If, in every moment of thought, one contemplates the two truths of suffering and its origin and gives rise to a great...

Compassion (*karuṇā*). Based on the two truths of the Path and Cessation, one gives rise to great loving-kindness (*maitrī*). One deeply contemplates the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*).

Out of pity for sentient beings who are deluded and confused, one employs various skillful means (*upāya*) to cause them to awaken. This extends throughout the realms of the ten directions without limit;
it continues until the end of the future without weariness or fatigue; and it seeks no reward of gratitude, no fame, nor hopes that others shall know of it.

Not perceiving subject and object is called the bodhisattva’s path of action (*karmapatha*). When condensed, these constitute the ten supreme wholesome deeds, both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
If, in every moment of thought, one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena: by means of the provisional, one realizes the real, such that principle and phenomenon are equal;

by means of the real, one manifests the provisional, such that the thousandfold distinctions of *tathatā* are quiescent yet constantly active. Thus, the myriad practices arise like clouds; through this activity, [one returns to stillness].
Ever quiescent, it is both a single limit and limitless. It does not form the notion of "one," nor does it form the notion of "all.
Yet, it is able to fully know that one is all, and all is one. Within a single hair-tip, the lands of atoms are not separated;

throughout the ten periods of past and present, they do not depart from the current thought-moment. The body pervades the ten directions without merging or dispersing; wisdom enters the three periods of time without...
Coming and going—this is called the path of action of the Buddha-realm. When subsumed, it constitutes the non-outflowing and non-non-outflowing, highest-grade (adhimātra) ten wholesome actions;
it is also termed the true, intermediate, non-outflowing, highest-grade ten wholesome actions.

Second, to clarify the four teachings: although the good and evil of the six classes of ordinary beings each have three grades, because they possess false attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*), they are collectively termed "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) and are all that which is to be remedied by the Tripitaka Teaching. As for the untainted (*anāsrava*) ten wholesome paths of the two vehicles:

if they know non-self through analytical discernment, they belong to the Tripitaka Teaching; if they know non-self through direct realization of the essence, they belong to the Shared Teaching. Bodhisattvas likewise [possess] outflows...

Regarding the ten wholesome paths of action that are untainted (*anāsrava*): if one arouses compassion by taking as an object the four truths of arising and ceasing, they belong to the Tripitaka Teaching and are termed "tainted.
If one arouses compassion by taking as an object the four truths of non-arising, they belong to the Shared Teaching and are termed "untainted.
If one arouses compassion by taking as an object the immeasurable four truths, they belong to the Distinct Teaching and are termed [also...]
Regarding outflows (*āsrava*) and non-outflows (*anāsrava*): if one arouses compassion by taking the unconditioned Four Noble Truths as an object, it belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

From the perspective of the "double negation" (*shuangzhe*), it is termed "neither outflow nor non-outflow"; from the perspective of the "double illumination" (*shuangzhao*), it may also be termed "both outflow and non-outflow.
As for the "superior-superior grade of the ten wholesome paths" within the Buddha-realm that is neither outflow nor non-outflow, it properly belongs to the Perfect Teaching. This is because...
This perfect understanding permeates all phenomena, such that even the three preceding teachings and the highest grade of the ten unwholesome actions are transformed into non-outflowing,
non-inflowing, supreme-grade wholesome states. Just as there is no grass or wood that does not contain fire,
and no solid ice that is not ultimately water, so too, when names are established according to their meaning, this is specifically termed "neither outflowing nor non-outflowing."
It is good. It is also called the "supremely pure, untainted, and wondrously wholesome" within the ultimate truth.

If one were to establish a definition based on its name, it could be termed "supremely high-grade wholesome," yet it could also be termed "supremely high-grade unwholesome," as in the expression "slaying the father of ignorance."

Furthermore, it can be called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), and it can also be called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), because it continuously flows forth as an ocean of all merits, never coming to an end.
It can be called "neither with nor without outflows," and it can also be called "both with and without outflows."
By illuminating both the tainted (*āsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) simultaneously, all phenomena (*dharma*) tend toward the tainted and the untainted.

Regarding the three insights (*vidyā*) and six identities (*samyaktva-niyāma*): since these are discussed based on the perfect reality that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there are no phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma.
From the highest Buddha-realm down to the lowest hell, all karmic natures are nothing other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). [The state of] madness...
If wisdom does not discern this, one will indiscriminately claim sainthood and invite calamity—like touching a treasure in the dark, thereby injuring the body and losing one's life.

Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish the six stages through cultivation to avoid falling into grave transgressions. Although the beginning and end of these six positions are clearly distinct, the nature of phenomena within their activity remains without increase or decrease;
thus, they are said to be "identical. That the nature of phenomena is identical to the nature of activity is precisely the ultimate nature of activity.
Regarding the nature [of karma]: The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states, "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it can universally produce all realms of rebirth. It is only that those who are deluded do not know this themselves. To know this nature of karma is the stage of "Identity with Name" (*mingzi ji*).

To contemplate this nature of karma so as to perfectly subdue the five stages of dwelling is the stage of "Identity with Contemplative Practice" (*guanheng ji*). When coarse defilements first fall away and the six sense faculties become pure, this is the stage of... [the text continues].

The "identity of similarity" (*sādharmya-ekatva*) is when true illumination is developed within this nature of karma; this constitutes the "partial realization of identity" (*pradeśa-prativedha-ekatva*).

When this nature of karma is exhausted without remainder, it constitutes the "ultimate identity" (*atyanta-ekatva*). This concludes the section on the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) belonging to the ten realms.

Regarding the fourth point, the synthesis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*), there are also three meanings: first, synthesis by way of the vertical; second, synthesis by way of the horizontal;
and third, synthesis by way of a single thought-moment that is neither horizontal nor vertical. First, regarding synthesis by way of the vertical:

the six elements and the paths of karma produced through causes and conditions constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The paths of karma of the two vehicles, wherein causes and conditions are themselves empty, constitute [the ultimate truth].
The true reality (*tattva*) consists of the karmic paths of the bodhisattvas, which are conventionally designated as immeasurable; this forms the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The karmic paths of the Buddha-realm profoundly penetrate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of both transgression and merit; this forms the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). Second, regarding the horizontal synthesis: the karmic paths of the ten realms.
Each and every one is without exception produced by causes and conditions; each and every one is none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Regarding the third point, the synthesis within a single thought-moment: if we take this very present thought-moment and differentiate the karmic paths of the ten realms, how can it be called "vertical"?
If the karmic paths of the ten realms are but a single thought-moment, how can it be called "horizontal"? It is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet it is both horizontal and vertical.
It is clearly manifest. It unifies the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is inconceivable; there is nothing that is not dharma-nature, and thus it is the Middle Way (*madhyama*).

It is neither horizontal nor vertical, and thus it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Horizontal and vertical manifestations are clearly manifest, layer upon layer and inexhaustible, and thus it is the provisional (*prajñapti*). The second explanation of karma is concluded.
The third explanation of "retribution" (*vipāka*) is also fourfold. First, the explanation of the meaning; second, the discernment of its categories; third, the attribution to the ten realms;
and fourth, the conclusion that it is identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Regarding the first, the explanation of the meaning: "retribution" refers to karmic retribution.

It is called a "fruit" (*phala*) in contrast to its cause, and it is called "retribution" as it compensates for karma; thus, the fruit is itself the retribution. Furthermore, in terms of what is induced by the causal habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*), it is termed the "habituated fruit" (*vāsanā-phala*); in terms of retribution...

That which is produced by causes is termed the "fruition of retribution" (*vipākaphala*). Thus, the fruit belongs to the "perfected seed" (*paripūraka-bīja*), while the retribution itself belongs to the "conditioned seed" (*pratyaya-bīja*).

Furthermore, there are two meanings of "retribution": first, that which is produced by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is termed "general retribution"; second, that which is produced by completing karma (*paripūrakakarman*) is termed "specific retribution.
General retribution is called the "true maturation fruit" (*vipāka-phala*) and belongs to the eighth consciousness; specific retribution is called...

The fruit born of maturation (*vipākaja*) belongs to a portion of the first six consciousnesses that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). It consists solely of the experiencing of pleasure and pain and does not initiate karma.
One should know that there are two types—general and specific—and both are termed "retribution" (*vipāka*).

Regarding these mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced as retribution in response to causes, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) belongs to the mind (*citta*), while that which responds to the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) belongs to the seeds of the cognitive cause (*pariccheda-hetu*). [This is] the specific [classification].

It is termed "fruit" (*phala*). The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) belongs to form (*rūpa*). That which compensates for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) belongs to the seeds of the contributing causes (*pratyaya-hetu*);

it is specifically termed "retribution" (*vipāka*). Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Such is the fruit; such is the retribution. Furthermore, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is the "suchness-nature" (*tathatā-svabhāva*);

the objective aspect is the "suchness-characteristic" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*); and the internal self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), upon which these two aspects depend, is the "suchness-essence" (*tathatā-vastu*). Taking the entire essence...
Regarding the function of accomplishment: since this function has no separate essence, it is said to be neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct.
Second, regarding the classification of types: the retributive fruits of the three miserable realms (trāya) summoned by the ten non-virtues are exclusively suffering.

Among the two classes of hungry ghosts and animals, there may be slight pleasure. In the realms of asuras and humans, suffering and pleasure coexist. In the celestial realm, there is only pleasure. Furthermore, concerning...

The five types of feeling are as follows: In the uninterrupted [realms], there are only painful feelings and neutral feelings; the same applies to those ghosts and animals who experience extreme suffering.
In the interrupted [realms], they may also possess sorrowful feelings, or perhaps slight joy and slight pleasure.

Ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and the gods of the desire realm all possess all five feelings. This is because when the gods and asuras are at war, there is sorrow and pain. However, in the northern continent (Uttarakuru)...

When a person does not reckon things as "mine," there is no feeling of sorrow or suffering. In the first dhyāna, one is free from the faculty of sorrow; in the second dhyāna, one is free from the faculty of suffering;
in the third dhyāna, one is free from the faculty of joy; there remains only pleasure and equanimity. In the fourth dhyāna, one is free from the faculty of pleasure.
From here up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is only the feeling of equanimity. These five [levels] all involve tainted (*sāsrava*) feelings. As for the Two Vehicles...

Quiescence is bliss. To transcend the five types of sensation and to have no sensation whatsoever is called "right reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*), and it is also called "untainted reception" (*anāsrava-vedanā*).
The Bodhisattva does not accept the right reception of the two vehicles; rather, he transcends the conventional through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to take them as his dharma-bliss.
This is called "feeling that is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). It is called "with-outflows" because it manifests the experience of birth and death;
it is called "without-outflows" because it is not defiled by the faults and afflictions of birth and death. The Buddhas do not undergo any feelings whatsoever.

Because they have nothing to receive, they constantly experience the Middle Way—the Dharma-joy that accords with the nature of reality—which is called "neither with-outflows nor without-outflows. It is not...

Because it is identical with the four luxuriant [branches], it is not *āsrava* (outflow); because it is not identical with the four withered [branches], it is not *anāsrava* (non-outflow). The inclusion of the four bases within two is as previously explained.

Furthermore, without discussing the fivefold classification of the *āsrava* and *anāsrava* of the five feelings (*vedanā*), one may judge them all in total by the two terms "suffering" and "pleasure," which encompasses everything without exception. One should know that suffering and pleasure are merely divisions of one's own mind.
In truth, there are no phenomena external to the mind. Why is this? The extreme suffering of Avīci is known by all the world;
yet, for a Bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who sports with great compassion, taking upon himself the sufferings of sentient beings is regarded as joy.
Thus, it is said that Devadatta was a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). If this state is like the third dhyāna, how could he have actually committed the crime of parricide?
Can one truly obtain such [happiness]? Now, maggots dwelling in a latrine, writhing and emerging and submerging, also consider themselves happy.
Flies fly toward stench; moths vie to rush into fire; dogs devour filth—all of these consider themselves happy. Yet, when viewed from the perspective of human beings, [they are not].

Unable to endure such suffering, humans are mired in the coarse and debased five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), remaining in a state of delusion and intoxication; when the gods look upon them, they appear like a latrine of excrement.
Even the five sensory objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are increasingly exquisite and wondrous, yet when viewed by those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are no less than lethal poison.
The physical form of Brahmā is radiant with brilliant light; those in the realm of empty space loathe it, regarding it as like a festering sore or poison.
The four meditative absorptions of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) consider themselves subtle and refined, yet Arhats view them as dull darkness.

The outflow-free, unconditioned samādhis of the Śrāvakas are rebuked by Bodhisattvas as being like rotten seeds. The supernatural powers of the Mahāsattvas allow for effortless coming and going; [all these]...
The Buddha views them as if they were children at play; thus we know that the sentient beings of the nine realms all take suffering to be pleasure.
The lower their station, the more inferior their pleasures become. Looking down from above, one knows that what those below take for pleasure is, in its very essence, suffering.

Only the Buddha has exhausted the sentiments of both suffering and pleasure, realizing that the realm of suffering and the realm of pleasure are, in truth, nothing but the single reality-mark (*dharmatā*).

The absence of suffering and pleasure is what is called "Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*). For now, however, following the conventional understanding of the nine realms, that which accords with and satisfies the body and mind is termed a "retribution of pleasure," while that which opposes and harms the body and mind is termed a "retribution of suffering.
These retributions of suffering and pleasure are each summoned by their own corresponding wholesome or unwholesome karma. Part two, the analysis of categories, is concluded.

The three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) pertain to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). They are further divided into three parts: first, an explanation of the ten realms; second, an explanation of the four teachings (*caturvidha-śāsana*);

and third, an explanation of the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yāvadbhāvikatā*). First, regarding the explanation of the ten realms: the retributive offenses within the realm of hell (*naraka-dhātu*) are entirely summoned by the ten grave evil deeds (*daśākuśala-karma*) of the highest grade.
Their substance consists of coarse and harsh physical and mental forms. Those that are heavy reside beneath the great earth; those that are light...

Those who dwell amidst the various mountains of darkness experience only suffering and no joy. The retribution for the dharma-realm of animals is summoned by the ten non-virtuous actions of medium grade;
the retribution for the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts is summoned by the ten non-virtuous actions of inferior grade.

Both take a base and degraded physical and mental constitution as their essence. Within these realms, there are distinct retributions of both suffering and joy, differing according to three grades and nine categories.
This is the retribution for full karma, termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Its manifestations are not uniform and cannot be described in detail.
As for their abodes, they range through mountain ranges, human realms, the waters, lands, and skies, as well as the realm of the *asuras*. Their retributive dwelling is in the great ocean;

their enjoyments resemble those of the gods and are thus pleasant, yet they suffer from the three times of [conflict with] weapons. As for the realm of humans, their retribution lies within the four continents. For a time...
At that time, the five desires constitute pleasure, while birth, old age, sickness, and death constitute suffering. Within the Dharma-realm of the heavenly path, there are three [realms]:
first, the desire realm; second, the form realm; and third, the formless realm. In the desire realm, there are six heavens: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Either taking the ten superior wholesome actions as the cause, or the eightfold precepts and fast for one day and night as the cause,
or lifelong refuge in the Triple Gem and the diligent observance of the single precept against killing as the cause, one obtains a superior form and mind as a karmic retribution.
Those who dwell in the interior of Mount Sumeru are the gods of the second realm, the Trāyastriṃśa.

They take as their cause either the superior practice of the ten wholesome paths, or the eightfold precepts observed for one day and night, or the lifelong observance of the three refuges along with the two precepts of non-killing and non-stealing.
As a result of this retribution, they obtain an exceptionally sublime form and mind, and dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Both of these [groups]...
They take mastery over the five desires as their pleasure, and the battles with the asuras as well as the manifestation of the five signs of decline as their suffering.

Third is the Yāma Heaven, which is translated here as "Time-Portion. Its causes are either the superior practice of the ten wholesome paths combined with the cultivation of seated meditation, or the observance of the eight precepts for one day and one night, or the lifelong taking of the three refuges and the diligent maintenance of the three pure precepts.

Due to this cause, they obtain a superior form and mind as a karmic retribution. Eighty thousand *yojanas* away from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a ground like clouds suspended in the void, abiding with brilliant clarity.
It does not rely on the sun or moon; their bodies possess radiance. When the flowers open, it is day;

when the flowers close, it is night. This is the fourth heaven, Tuṣita, which means "Contentment" (*zīzhú*). Alternatively, it refers to those who practice the ten wholesome deeds of the highest grade...

Taking as causes either the attainment of subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-vihāra*), or the eightfold precepts for one day and night, or lifelong taking of the three refuges and the diligent observance of the four precepts, one obtains a superior form and mind as a karmic retribution.

Sixteen thousand *yojanas* above the Yāma Heaven, there is a ground like clouds that abides in mid-air; this is the fifth heaven, the Nirmāṇarati (Heaven of Delighting in Emanations). Or, [there are those who attain it] through the superior grade of the ten [wholesome paths of action].
This goodness is caused by both the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the desire realm and, alternatively, by the eightfold precepts observed for one day and one night.
As a result, one obtains an exceptionally superior form and mind. Thirty-two hundred thousand *yojanas* away from Tuṣita Heaven, there is a ground like clouds.

They abide in mid-air. As for the sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven: its cause is either the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths combined with the attainment of the *anāgamya* (uninterrupted) concentration, or the eightfold precepts observed for one day and night, and so forth. By retribution, they obtain an exceptionally sublime form and mind.
Sixty-four hundred thousand *yojanas* above the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, there is a ground like clouds that abides in mid-air.

These four [realms] likewise take as their pleasure the mutual superiority attained through mastery over the five objects of desire, and take as their suffering the manifestation of the five signs of decay.
The realm of form consists of eighteen heavens, divided into four dhyānas. The first dhyāna has three heavens:

first, the Brahmakāyika; second, the Brahmapurohita; and third, the Mahābrahmā. They all share the fivefold qualities of the fundamental first dhyāna as their cause. Alternatively, [the text continues:]
Taking pure filial piety as the cause, or taking profound and heavy shame and remorse as the cause, or taking profound and heavy compassion as the cause,
or taking the reunification of a split Saṃgha as the cause, one obtains a retributive purity of form and mind.
One hundred twenty-eight million yojanas beyond the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, there is ground like clouds that abides suspended in mid-air.
The lifespan lasts for one great kalpa, though there are also those who die prematurely. Being free from sorrow and pure is happiness;

falling away at the time of death is suffering. The three heavens of the second dhyāna are: first, Parīttābha (Limited Light); second, Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light); and third, Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound).
Taking the four factors of the fundamental second dhyāna as their cause, they obtain a retributive pure form and mind.
Two million five hundred and sixty thousand yojanas above the first dhyāna heaven, there is a ground like clouds that abides suspended in mid-air.
The lifespan reaches eight great kalpas, though there may also be those who die prematurely. Being free from suffering and pure is happiness;

falling away at the time of death is suffering. The three heavens of the third dhyāna are: first, the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parittaśubha); second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha); and third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
Taking the five factors of the fundamental third dhyāna as their cause, they obtain pure matter and mind as karmic retribution.
Five million one hundred twelve thousand yojanas above the Second Dhyāna Heaven, there is ground like clouds that abides suspended in mid-air.

The lifespan is sixty-four kalpas, though there are also those who die prematurely. The sublime bliss free from joy is considered happiness; the falling away at the time of death is considered suffering.

The nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna are further divided into three categories: first, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); second, non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*); and third, noble ones who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
There are three heavens for ordinary worldlings: first, the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*); second, the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Vṛhatphala*); and third, [the Heaven of Great Fruit].
The Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven likewise takes as its cause the four factors of the fundamental fourth dhyāna. It is retributively obtained as a tranquil and immovable form-and-mind.
It is situated one million twenty-four hundred thousand yojanas above the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna, following the palaces of its inhabitants.
They abide serenely in the midst of empty space, and as there is no ground like that of clouds, it is also called the Heaven of No-Cloud (Anabhraka).
Their lifespan is five hundred great kalpas, though some may die prematurely. They take the purity of equanimity and mindfulness as their bliss.
At the time of death, falling away and descending is suffering. There is one class of non-Buddhists known as the "Non-conceptualizers" (asaṃjñika).

Taking the meditative absorption of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) as their cause, they obtain through karmic retribution a state of tranquility and immobility of both form and mind. After half an eon has passed, the first six evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) all cease to function;
only the seventh and eighth consciousnesses continue to operate in mutual dependence, with the eighth being able to maintain [the continuity].
The form-body (rūpakāya) abides for a long time; its lifespan is five hundred kalpas, though some may die prematurely.

At the time of death, one is certain to fall back into suffering and will not return to the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*): first, Avṛha; second, Atapa; third, Sudarśana; fourth, Sudṛśa; and fifth, Akaniṣṭha.
These beings alike employ untainted (*anāsrava*) permeation to augment the four dhyānas, taking their former karma as the cause, and thus obtain the retribution of tranquility.
The formless and immovable states of mind and matter cannot be seen by ordinary beings of the four *dhyānas*. Their lifespan may last for a thousand *kalpas*, or even up to ten thousand *kalpas*;
they experience eternal bliss without falling back, yet this remains suffering because they have not yet transcended the three realms. The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of four heavens:

first, the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), which takes the concentration on space as its cause; their lifespan is twenty thousand *kalpas*. Second, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
The gods of the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness take the concentration of infinite consciousness as their cause; their lifespan is forty thousand kalpas.
The gods of the Heaven of Nothingness take the concentration of nothingness as their cause; their lifespan is sixty thousand kalpas.

The gods of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception take the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their cause; their lifespan is eighty thousand kalpas. Having extinguished form and preserved the mind, there remains only...
Even for those with subtle feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is premature death;

likewise, they take delight in escaping the cage of form, yet at the time of death, their falling away constitutes suffering. Within the *śrāvaka* dharma-realm, there are the four paths and four fruits.

The first fruit takes the seeds of untainted wisdom regarding the emptiness of birth as its cause, and the cultivation of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation as its condition, thereby giving rise to the realization of the emptiness of birth.
Non-conceptual wisdom suddenly severs the seeds of the delusions of discrimination within the three realms and directly realizes a portion of the true suchness manifested by the emptiness of persons;
this is termed "unconditioned cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*). It is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).

Although his body still remains among humans or in the heavens, one should know that these human and celestial bodies are still tainted (*sāsrava*), being the remaining retribution of prior karma, and are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is the retribution. The second fruit takes the profound contemplation of the Truth as its cause;

it gradually severs six of the nine grades of innate afflictions (*kṣipta-kleśa*) of the desire realm and directly realizes the unconditioned state of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) for those six grades.

Its body remains among humans or in the heavens, and because it is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), it is a retribution summoned by karma. The third fruit likewise takes the profound contemplation of the Truth as its cause.

Having completely exhausted the remaining three grades of afflictions of the desire realm and further realized the unconditioned state of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those three grades, his body remains either among humans or in the heavens;
because it is still tainted (*sāsrava*), it is retribution summoned by karma. Once he has cast off this body of the desire realm...

The retribution occurs in the first dhyāna; because it is still with outflows (*sāsrava*), karma brings about this retribution. If the afflictions of the first dhyāna have been severed, the retribution occurs in the second dhyāna.
If the afflictions of the second dhyāna have been severed, the retribution occurs in the third dhyāna. If the afflictions of the third dhyāna have been severed...

The retribution [for these] resides among the five Non-returner heavens of the fourth dhyāna. If one has already severed the afflictions of the fourth dhyāna, the retribution resides in the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana).

If one has already severed the afflictions of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the retribution resides in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana). If one has already severed the afflictions of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the retribution resides in the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).

If one has already severed the afflictions of the Sphere of Nothingness, the retribution resides in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Up to this point is what is called [the range].
The fruit of *anāgāmin* is entirely a retribution summoned by contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma; it is not the retribution of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.

Whether among humans or devas, if one can further sever the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one is termed a candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).

If one has already completely severed the afflictions of thought of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one universally realizes the eighty-one grades of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called the fruit of arhatship. At that time, one is said to dwell in *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
This body still remains among humans or in the heavens; since this body is also contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is the residual retribution of past karma.
When this human or celestial body spontaneously perishes, and one no longer undergoes further birth within the three realms, at that time one is said to dwell in *nirvāṇa without remainder*.

[The character] "pan" [is used]. If one relies on the provisional teaching, there is no retribution or fruit at all. If one relies on the definitive teaching, there is a pure land outside the triple world.
Those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who claim to have entered nirvāṇa are born therein and receive the dharma-nature body;
they do not undergo birth through the segmentation of life. One should know that this is precisely the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, which is also called the "Three Kinds."

This is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). To discuss suffering and pleasure in general: for one in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the permanent closing of the gates to the three evil realms is pleasure, while not yet having severed desire-attachment (*kāma-rāga*) is suffering.
For one in the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the gradual thinning of the tendencies of desire is pleasure, while not yet being free from the fetters of desire is suffering.

For those in the third fruit and the candidates for the fourth fruit (*anāgāmin*), never again returning [to lower realms] is pleasure, while not yet being free from the realms of form and formlessness is suffering.

Being bound is suffering. Regarding the four fruits [of the śrāvaka] while still remaining in the state of *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder): to have permanently severed the bonds of the seeds is happiness; not yet having exhausted the bonds of the fruits is suffering.
When one abides in the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder), according to the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*), there is then forever neither suffering nor happiness.

According to the ultimate teaching (*nītārtha*), however, transcending the triple world is happiness, while sinking into emptiness and lingering in quiescence is suffering. This is the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the realm (*dhātu*), it does not establish separate fruits, yet there are two categories.

The first consists of those of the *pratyekabuddha* lineage who, having cultivated merit and practiced the causes for four births and one hundred kalpas, have matured their untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and attained the Way among humans.

If they encounter a Buddha’s era, they enter the ranks of the *śrāvakas* and are likewise called *pratyekabuddhas*; if they encounter an era without a Buddha, they are called *pratyekabuddha-buddhas*. The second consists of those *śrāvakas* at the beginning...
In their final seventh birth, they exhaust [their defilements] and receive a human body; encountering a world where no Buddha exists, they are likewise called Pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the two types of suffering and pleasure—those with remainder and those without remainder—they are explained identically to that in the section on Śrāvakas. As for the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu, it must be distinguished according to the four teachings.
If one speaks of a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, they have not yet severed any afflictions, but merely [rely upon] the Four Great Vows and the Six...
Taking the ten supreme wholesome deeds as the cause, one brings about the sublime retribution of form and mind within the realms of humans and devas.

One is not born among the three evil destinies or the various difficult states, such as the formless realm. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, this refers to the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi).
The retribution for those on the stages of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka*) and the Thin Ground (*tanubhūmi*) is equivalent to that of the first and second fruits (*phala*).

The retribution for those on the ground of freedom from desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*) is equivalent to the third fruit. From the ground of having already accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*) onwards, or for those in whom wisdom is predominant, their retribution regarding suffering and pleasure is discussed in terms of the four fruits, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the states with and without remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa*). However, they are born in lands of skillful means and do not sink [into the lower realms].
To dwell in emptiness and stillness is merely not yet to realize the dharma-nature of the Middle Way; one has not yet escaped the suffering of the death and rebirth of transformation.

Alternatively, for those in whom compassion is predominant, they sustain their habitual tendencies to moisten their rebirth, returning once more to the triple world to manifest the same fruits of retribution—suffering and joy—as those of the six realms, yet these are not actually the outflows of tainted suffering and joy, because they are not driven by karma. If [one were] distinct...

In teaching the Bodhisattvas, those in the stage of the ten faiths are the same as the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka. From the first abode through the sixth abode, they are likewise the same as the first, second, and third fruits [of the Śrāvaka path].
From the seventh abode onward, up to the ten directions [of the ten dedications], they are also distinguished by their wisdom and compassion;
at the time of ascending to the first bhūmi, they partially realize the Middle Way Dharmakāya and eternally dwell in the land of true recompense without obstruction.
This is also called the partially realized *dharmadhātu* of eternal quiescent light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*).

Up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), all take the retributive fruit of the Middle Way as bliss, while the fact that the transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted constitutes suffering.

They manifest partial forms and scattered shadows throughout the worlds of the six destinies and four modes of birth, as well as throughout the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*), displaying various sufferings identical to those of the six ordinary beings and the two classes of sages.

Pleasure and pain are both not truly pleasure or pain. If a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching, while within the five ranks (*pañcāvasthā*), receives the retributive bodies of humans or devas, is already able to understand that the true nature of suffering and pleasure is identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle.

From the first stage of faith through the sixth stage of faith, their retribution may be similar to that of those in the first, second, or third fruits of the *śrāvaka* path, yet their understanding is forever different. From the seventh stage of faith through the tenth stage of faith, or...
In the stage of expedient means (*upāya*), their retribution is the same as that of the Shared Teaching (*pṛthagjana-śrāvaka-yāna*), yet their understanding is eternally different.

Or, while in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), their retribution is the same as that of the Shared Teaching with an emphasis on compassion (*karuṇā*), yet their understanding is likewise eternally different.

Upon ascending to the first *bhūmi*, they partially realize the Tathāgata’s single body that is infinitely manifold, and they dwell perpetually in the Pure Land of Realized Reward and Adornment (*vipāka-saṃbhoga-vyūha-kṣetra*), which is also called the partially realized Land of Tranquil Light (*śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*).

From the Earth [Stage] up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they divide their forms and disperse their shadows throughout the three lower lands, manifesting the suffering and pleasure of the nine realms;
yet these are not actual suffering and pleasure. Regarding the Buddha-dharma realm, there are four types according to the teachings:

the fruit-Buddha of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) Teaching must be a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Separate or Perfect Stages, or a manifestation of Sublime Enlightenment (*vimalā-bodhi*). It is provisionally said that the birth-body (*janmakāya*) exists.

The report of [the Buddha] having outflows is merely a demonstration of conformity with the state of an Arhat. In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Buddha-stage is shown to reside in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
yet this is also not a real, segmented body within the three realms, but must be a manifested transformation of one dwelling in the Perfect stage of a distinct level.

In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue) sits in the Lotus Treasury World (Padmagarbhaloka); this too is what is seen according to the capacity of those with great faculties. It is simply that...

Regarding the enjoyment-retribution [body], it takes the self-enjoyment [body] as its essential substance (*bhāva*). The various great bodhisattvas each transform themselves into objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) and perceive them for themselves.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the wondrous enlightenment is ultimately and perfectly manifested through the nature-merit; this is called the pure *dharmakāya*.
The *dharmatā* upon which it relies is called the "supremely superior grade" (*uttama-adhimātra*) land of eternal, quiescent, radiant purity. As for the cultivation-merit...
Ultimate fulfillment is called the Perfect Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). The environment upon which it relies is called the Pure Land of Supreme Superior Real Reward Adornment.
Nature and cultivation are non-dual; the reliance (the environment) and the supported (the body) are non-dual.

While they are non-dual, they are differentiated as two, such that the names "Dharmakāya" and "Saṃbhogakāya," and "reliance" and "supported," are spoken of as distinct. This is the most supreme and unsurpassed reward. First, this is clarified.
The ten realms are concluded.

Second, to clarify the four teachings: the various tainted retributions of suffering and pleasure within the dharma-realm of the six ordinary beings are merely objects to be remedied by the four teachings;
they are not themselves subsumed by the four teachings. Nevertheless, as phenomena produced through causes and conditions, they constitute the conventional truth of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zàngjiào).

That which is expounded by the Truths can also generally serve as the object of contemplation for all four teachings. Within the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), the retributions of outflow-free suffering and pleasure are precisely what is experienced by the nine types of persons across the four teachings:
namely, the four fruits of the *śrāvaka* vehicle; the *pratyekabuddha* of the *pratyekabuddha* and *pāramitā* (Shared) teachings;

the *pratyekabuddha*, the bodhisattva at the stage of "having completed the task" (*kṛtāvin*), and the three stages of worthies (*tri-kalyāṇa*) of the Distinct Teaching; and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching. [This also applies to] the Land of True Retribution.

The Land of No Obstruction is that which is realized through the Ten Stages and the Equal Wondrousness of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), as well as through the Ten Abidings, Ten Practices, Ten Transferences, Ten Stages, and the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).

Although it also partially realizes the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), from the perspective of principle applied to phenomena, it is collectively termed the Land of True Retribution (*bhūtavedanīya-vipāka*).

Alternatively, based on the sequential entry into realization within a single mind, one may distinguish between the pure and the impure; this is merely a provisional designation according to the path of the teachings.
This is a distinction. The Constant Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa-kṣetra*) is that which is realized by the Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Although it is also the perfect realization of the superior grade of True Retribution (*shibao*), because phenomena follow principle, it is collectively termed "Quiescent Light. Alternatively, one may distinguish between the pure and the defiled based on partial realization versus ultimate realization;
this is merely a differentiation made according to the two fruits of the Separate (*bie*) and Perfect (*yuan*) Teachings. Furthermore, the Treasury Teaching (*zangjiao*) clarifies...
The retributive fruits of the six realms are the truly existent *duḥkha-satya*. If suffering is extinguished, one realizes true emptiness;

it is not said that the four types of noble ones also possess such retribution. In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), the retributive fruits of the six realms are explained as the illusory *duḥkha-satya*.

If one penetrates the emptiness of illusions, there is no birth-and-death, nor is it said that there is retribution for the four types of noble ones. In the Distinct Teaching (*vaibhāṣika-yāna*), the six [realms]... [are explained...]
The retribution of the path is *paricchinna-śīti* (segmented birth and death). The retribution of the fruits of the Three Vehicles is *pariṇāmi-śīti* (transformative birth and death).

Both are termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). To eternally sever these two types of death and realize the true Middle Way, that which is realized is called True Suchness Nirvāṇa (*tathatā-nirvāṇa*), and that which realizes it is called the Bodhi of the Four Wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*).
The mental category associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is able to manifest self-enjoyment.
By means of the body and the land, one is able to maintain the perfect, untainted seeds until the end of the future, bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
This explains that there are four noble fruits of retribution. In the Perfect Teaching, the retributive phenomena of the ten realms are clarified:
when one suffering is all sufferings, and suffering is itself the Dharma-realm, then the extinction of one is the extinction of all; this is neither retribution nor non-retribution.
This explains the retributions of the ten realms. Second, the explanation of the four teachings is concluded.

Third, regarding the six stages of identity (*liu ji*): since we are speaking in accordance with the nature of reality based on the perfect and true [teaching], then every retribution of suffering and joy within the ten dharma-realms is none other than the *dharmadhātu* of the true aspect (*shixiang*).
It is immediately empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. I fear that those who are deluded and confused might...
[One] knows [this]. Clinging to the foul as pure, one remains settled in base habits and seeks no liberation. It is like pointing to ice and saying it is water;
yet if one does not seek its melting, the water will remain ice. How could that be fit for drinking? Therefore, one distinguishes between the contrary and the compliant by means of six principles.
For example, although ice has moisture as its nature, it constantly opposes that moist nature, remaining stubbornly solid and frozen. This is the principle of "identity" (li-ji).

It is likewise in the stage of "Position" (*wei*). Within the wondrous retributions of the ten realms, one neither recognizes nor knows them; this state of ignorance constitutes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), wherein one suffering is all sufferings.
In the stage of "Names" (*mingzi*), at the beginning of compliant cultivation, one clearly understands the retributive phenomena of the ten realms.
It is solely this single mind. It is like solid ice, which is in reality water; one never discards the ice to seek water elsewhere.

This is the initial recognition of the names of the retributive phenomena of the ten realms. Within the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), one relies on these names to observe and fully understand that each and every retributive phenomenon of the ten realms is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, thereby perfectly subduing the three delusions. As it says:

Holding ice in one's hand, one knows it is moist and wet; likewise, within the stage of semblance (*sādharmya-avasthā*), one deeply contemplates the retributive phenomena of the ten realms and gains deep faith that they are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, just as ice near warmth gradually loses its solid characteristics.

Within the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha-avasthā*), the reality-body of the three truths within the retributive phenomena of the ten realms manifests part by part, just as warmth melts ice, causing it to dissolve bit by bit.
Every part may be used for drinking. In the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), the retributive phenomena of the ten realms and the wondrous principle of the three truths are perfectly manifested;
it is like when the ice has completely vanished, leaving only water that can entirely be used for drinking.

Therefore, when the fruit of the three thousandfold world-system is perfected, all are termed "Eternal and Blissful. The latrine truly becomes a fragrant palace, and filth truly becomes exquisite food.
Evil sounds truly become songs of praise; poisonous drugs truly become nectar; swords and arrows truly become flower garlands;

and even such things as "if I approach the mountain of blades, the mountain of blades shall spontaneously shatter," or "if I approach the cauldron of fire, the cauldron of fire shall spontaneously vanish"—these are all the true enjoyments within the stage of partial realization of the ultimate state, which do not exceed the realization of [the nature of reality].
This is merely the principle and essence of the retributive dharma in which sentient beings are deluded; how could it rely upon the power of intentional mental activity or supernatural faculties?

The third section concludes the classification of the three fetters across the ten realms. The fourth section establishes that these very fetters are identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, which likewise comprises three points: first, the vertical classification of the fetters; second, the horizontal classification of the fetters.
Third, the summary by way of a single thought-moment, which is neither horizontal nor vertical. First, regarding the summary by way of the vertical:

the various retributions of suffering and pleasure belonging to the six classes of ordinary beings, as well as the remaining residual retributions of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and furthermore, all the physical bodies of Bodhisattvas who have newly awakened to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), are also outflowing (*sāsrava*) and thus constitute residual retributions.
The phrase "all belonging to phenomena produced by causes and conditions" is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of an Arhat, only the final three elements are termed untainted (*anāsrava*); the preceding fifteen elements are all tainted (*sāsrava*).
Based on this, it is also said that the Buddhas of the *tathāgatagarbha* and the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are the same as the Arhats.

Both the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the two vehicles enter the realm of Nirvāṇa and are born within the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*) to receive a body of transformation (*nairmāṇikakāya*).
This applies equally to Bodhisattvas of the distinct [teaching] at the thirty minds and those of the perfect [teaching] at the ten stages of faith, who are all born in the Land of Expedient Means.
The five aggregates, eighteen realms, and so forth that undergo transformation are all subsumed under the single phrase "immediately empty" and are encompassed by the True Truth (*tattva-satya*);

therefore, they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Abiding in the perfect stage of a distinct land, one abandons the body of segmented birth and receives a fruition-body in the Land of Real Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, through the power of compassion and vows, one manifests within the various lands of shared residence and skillful means throughout the ten directions.
It manifests the images of the ten dharma-realms, universally sharing in both suffering and pleasure, yet these are not actual suffering or actual pleasure.

This extends even to the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which should manifest the three lands—the land of retribution for past deeds, the land of skillful means, and the land of common dwelling—universally displaying the images of the ten dharma-realms.

All of these belong to the single phrase "the provisional" (*jia*) within the "wondrous conventional truth" (*miaosu-di*), and are therefore termed "both out-flowing and non-out-flowing. This is the wondrous [teaching] of the Perfect Vehicle (*yuanjiao*).

Awakening is the ultimate, perfect realization of the secret treasury of the three virtues—the subtle Dharma-body of the eternally tranquil light-land—as well as the separate ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfect ten abodes (*vihāra*), which constitute the partial realization of the body and land of the tranquil light of the three virtues;

these all belong to the single phrase "identical with the Middle" and are subsumed within the supreme truth of the Middle Way. Therefore, they are called "neither out-flowing nor non-out-flowing. Second, regarding...

Regarding "transverse bonds": whether they be outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing, suffering or pleasure, provisional or ultimate, all that exists within the ten realms—both the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*)—is, without exception, either produced by causes and conditions or manifested by causes and conditions;
thus it may also be termed "produced by causes and conditions. Since these are phenomena produced by causes and conditions, they must necessarily...

By the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are immediately [identical with] emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle. There is not a single form or a single mind that is not immediately identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle.
To explain this more precisely: the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants—within the realm of common residence are produced by causes and conditions within the world;
they are conditioned and tainted, and thus possess the characteristics of suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity. However, these various characteristics such as suffering...
There is nothing that is not immediately emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. The two types of retribution—the environment and the body—are not of the nature of分段 (fen-duan) birth;

rather, they are manifested by the causes and conditions within the realm of desire. Being unconditioned and untainted, they possess the very nature of suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.

Yet these various natures, such as suffering and the rest, are likewise without exception immediately emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This is the true retribution of the environment and the body.
The conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena produced by causes and conditions outside the realms (*dhātu*) possess the characteristics of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Yet these characteristics of permanence and so forth are likewise not apart from emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. The two retributions—the environment and its inhabitants—of the *śānta-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light) are manifested through causes and conditions outside the realms;
they are the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted nature of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. However, this permanence...
The nature of these [three truths] is likewise not non-identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Because its essence is real, it is called the "middle.
Because it is free from all marks, it is further called "emptiness. Because it is identical with all phenomena, it is further called "non-empty.
If one regards the unconditioned and untainted *śānta-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light) in comparison to that expedient unconditioned and untainted [state], then...
It would then merely be conditioned and outflowing (*saṃskṛta-sāsrava*). Third, regarding the threefold classification based on a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*):

since good and evil are distinguished solely with respect to a single thought-moment, and all karmas are likewise distinguished solely with respect to a single thought-moment, how could the two retributions—the environment and the body—of the ten realms ever transcend this present single thought-moment?
A single thought-moment is fundamentally without before or after; how, then, can it be called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*)?
A single thought-moment is fundamentally without two bodies; how, then, can it be called "horizontal"?

By deeply contemplating that the ten realms possessed within a single thought-moment—both the environment and its inhabitants—are neither horizontal nor vertical, one is able to simultaneously illuminate both the horizontal and the vertical with perfect clarity.

Yet, each instance of the horizontal and vertical is itself neither horizontal nor vertical. Why? Because the retributive phenomena of the ten realms are nothing other than this single thought-moment; thus, they are not [separate entities].
Horizontal is not vertical. That "one is empty and all are empty" is the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

When a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) possesses the retributions of the ten realms, it is horizontal though not horizontal; when a single thought-moment creates the retributions of the ten realms, it is vertical though not vertical.
"One is provisional and all are provisional" is the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Apart from this single thought-moment, there is nothing else that is possessed or created.

The retributive dharmas of the ten realms can be apprehended. Apart from these retributive dharmas of the ten realms, there is nothing else that can be found capable of possessing or creating even a single thought-moment;
it is solely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), solely the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
It is neither upright nor not upright; neither horizontal nor not horizontal. It is free from names and transcends marks, yet there are no names or marks to be freed from or transcended.
This is the Middle Truth within the inconceivable. The third explanation of retribution is complete. Thus concludes the first section, which explains the retribution of good and evil karma.

The second type of explanation, the combined interpretation (*samāsa-nirdeśa*), is further divided into six parts: first, an explanation based on the ten suchnesses; second, an explanation based on the twelve links of dependent origination;
third, an explanation based on the four truths; fourth, an explanation based on the two truths; fifth, an explanation based on the three truths; and sixth, an explanation based on the one truth.
Regarding the first, the explanation based on the ten suchnesses: good and evil are precisely the "suchness of nature" (*tathatā-svabhāva*); "nature" is defined by its quality of being unchanging.
Meaning: Goodness has the nature of being well-disciplined, compliant, and pure; it cannot be changed into evil. Evil has the nature of being coarse, violent, and defiled;
it cannot be changed into goodness. Each of the ten realms possesses its own seed-nature (*gotra*). Karma is precisely of this character:
when the intention is raised, the body is moved, and speech is uttered, there is a manifestation of the activities of the ten realms. Upon examining these...
They may be distinguished. Nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*) both rely upon form and mind (*se-xin*); form and mind are precisely this substance (*ti*).
These good and evil karmas each possess their own power and capacity, and each has its own structure; this is the power and the activity of the ten realms (*shi-jie*) as they are.
Good and evil, when considered in terms of nature, are the causes of the ten realms as they are. Since karma is considered in terms of characteristics, it is the ten [realms]... [as they are].

The realms (*dhātu*) are thus the conditions. "Retribution" refers to the ten realms, comprising both matter and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants; this is precisely the fruit and the retribution.

Nature and characteristics constitute the root, while fruit and retribution constitute the branches. Within the single emptiness, all things are empty; from beginning to end, there is no inherent nature.
Therefore, they are "emptiness" and so forth. One is provisional and all are provisional; from beginning to end they exist within one another. By beholding the root, one can know the branches;

by beholding the branches, one can recognize the root. Therefore, they are "provisionality" and so forth. One is the center and all are the center; from beginning to end, their principle is identical.
That which is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the true nature (*bhūtadharmatā*), and even the true fruit (*bhūta-phala*) and true retribution (*bhūta-vipāka*), is therefore the Middle Way.

Because words cannot manifest [this reality] instantaneously, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle are distinguished sequentially. In reality, they do not exist as vertical, horizontal, simultaneous, or separate entities.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true mark of all phenomena. This is what is meant by "all phenomena are thus."
They are equal. This sutra states: "Those who wish to enter the Mahāyāna should first know the fundamental practice to be undertaken at the outset.
That is to say, they should cultivate faith and understanding by relying upon the single reality realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*). As for this "single reality realm":
This is precisely the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; therefore, it can be explained by means of the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*).
