13. Distinguishing the wise ordinary persons outside the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). They believe in the true reality (*tathatā*) of the ultimate fruit;

seeking this principle, they give rise to the ten minds of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*), becoming free from the net of doubt for themselves and performing divinations for others in accordance with the marks of the wheel.

14. Distinguishing the wise ordinary persons within the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*). In the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), they primarily practice the entry into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while concurrently practicing the provisional and the middle.

In the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), one correctly practices the provisional and practices the middle as a secondary focus. In the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), one correctly practices the middle and fully possesses the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Having no doubt or regret oneself, one is able to resolve the doubts of others and universally knows the karmic retributions of good and evil within the ten realms; yet, one cannot know that each and every thing is itself the middle.
Fifteenth: regarding the wisdom of the Middle Way in the distinct ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), once one has realized the true reality (*tathatā*), one illuminates both simultaneously.
The two extremes are spontaneously quiescent yet constantly illuminating. In the first bhūmi, a single thought-moment illumines a hundred worlds;

in the second bhūmi, a single thought-moment illumines a thousand worlds, and so forth, increasing progressively until it cannot be fully described. Sixteenth, regarding the distinct wisdom of wondrous enlightenment:

seated within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*), responding to the capacities of beings throughout the dharma-realm, the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) illumines universally both horizontally and vertically. Below...
The earth cannot fathom its limits. XVII. Regarding those with the five grades of perfect wisdom: even an ordinary person bound by all fetters can know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury;
though they possess only the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye, and they have no doubt-net within themselves.

It is not necessary [to use] the wheel diagram for resolving the doubts of others, yet it may also be employed for that purpose. Furthermore, when practicing various samādhis oneself, one may likewise rely on the wheel to seek resolution.
For example, the Great Master Yongming, though he had already awakened to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), nevertheless composed the *Zuochan* and *Wanshan* manuals.

One should know that the method of drawing lots (*nianqian*) originates from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (specifically the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, *Yuánjué jīng*), and is consistent with the present wheel diagrams and...
The *Abhiṣeka-divyopāya-sūtra* is identical in name to the *Saddharma*; it is not comparable to worldly divination. 18.

The wise ordinary person within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) has purified the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddha*). They are able to spontaneously resolve the web of doubts throughout the trichiliocosm and discern the capacities of beings in the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) without error.
19. The wise one who has partially realized the forty-first stage (*ekacatvāriṃśad-bhūmi-pradeśa-prativedha-jñānin*) is at the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*).
Sublime wisdom is like the newly risen moon; its radiance already illuminates everything without exception. How much more so when it gradually increases until the fourteenth night!
As for the twenty-fold, perfectly sublime, awakened Buddha’s ultimate wisdom, it is like the moon on the fifteenth night.
Both essence and appearance are perfectly complete; the Dharma-realm is transparently clear. There is nothing left uncomprehended, whether vertically or horizontally.

Vertically, one contemplates the distant past as if it were this very day, and regarding all events of the future, the bestowal of predictions is never erroneous. Horizontally, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is known by its count.
Whether pines are straight or thorns are crooked, whether cranes are white or crows are black—all their fundamental causes and conditions are fully understood. By means of this...
To state it briefly: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom instantaneously reflects all things; the Wisdom of Equality universally enters all things;
the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation thoroughly understands causes and conditions; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks simultaneously and universally responds to all, without discrimination.
It is not that there is no discernment; it is without sequence, yet not without sequence.
Even the wisdom possessed up to the tenth stage is like the soil of Jambudvīpa compared to the soil of a great trichiliocosm—it is inconceivable and indescribable.
This is the ultimate wisdom of divination and examination. Now, as for the Great Being Kṣitigarbha, he may be [the embodiment of] the Perfect [Teaching].
The wisdom of equal enlightenment, or the perfectly sublime awakened wisdom, is fundamentally lofty yet its traces are hidden below, such that it cannot be fathomed or known.
Because his compassion for this land was profound and his karmic conditions deep, the Great Sage Śākyamuni caused those of firm and pure faith to request the teaching of this Dharma.
This enables ordinary beings on the vast ground to suddenly cast off the net of doubt by relying upon it, while also extensively elucidating the single reality.

Regarding the "Spheres of Experience" (*viṣaya*): it provides a detailed exposition of two types of contemplative paths as skillful means for progress, and further skillfully explains the profound Dharma to comfort the deluded masses.
Being in true accord with reality and free from the fault of contradiction, it enables those at the initial stage of the name-only path.
It is universally able to examine and discern the karmic retributions of good and evil within the ten realms, whether in terms of phenomena or principle, exhaustively and without exception.
Why is the wondrousness of this Dharma gate such? Furthermore, one should know that these karmic retributions of good and evil are themselves the wondrousness of the object (*viṣaya*).

Divination and contemplation (*jiantan*) constitute the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna-sauṣṭhava*). To harmonize with the object through wisdom and cultivate the two contemplations constitutes the excellence of practice (*caryā-sauṣṭhava*).

To achieve the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the patience of conformity (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) constitutes the excellence of stage (*avasthā-sauṣṭhava*). Through the fulfillment of the dharma of faith, one becomes a Buddha.

One becomes a Buddha by perfecting the Dharma of understanding; one becomes a Buddha by realizing the perfection of the Dharma; and one becomes a Buddha because all meritorious practices are fulfilled.
This is also the excellence of the stage and the excellence of the three dharmas, for it is the fulfillment of the secret treasury of the three virtues that abide together from beginning to end.
Abiding spontaneously in the three virtues, it is quiescent yet eternally illuminating; whenever there is a stimulus, there is a response—this is "responsive resonance" (ganying).
"Excellent! Furthermore, I teach sentient beings to practice repentance and contemplate the Dharma-body as that which can be invoked.
If one can do so with a sincere heart, whatever they divined will be auspicious and all their requests will be fulfilled;

they may even enter the Samādhi of One Practice and see countless Buddhas—all through the wondrous power of resonance and response. At that time, I manifested my body according to the needs of those to be saved."

Either he manifests various supernatural transformations through his supernormal powers, or he causes others to recollect their own past lives—this is the excellence of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

Or again, according to their inclinations, he preaches various profound and essential teachings, even skillfully explaining the deep Dharma so that they may be freed from timidity and weakness—this is the excellence of his teaching (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*). When sentient beings hear the Dharma, their doubts are removed and faith is born—this is...
The excellence of the retinue is such that one can obtain profound and great benefit, gradually attaining Buddhahood; this is the excellence of merit and benefit.
If the excellence of the traces of realization is understood, the fundamental excellence is not remote; therefore, the Buddha praised him, saying:

"This son of good family, since first generating the mind of enlightenment, has already passed through immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and has long been able to cross over [the ocean of suffering]."

The ocean of *vibhū* (all-knowledge) is fully replete with merit; yet, by the power of the sovereign freedom of his original vows, he manifests transformations through skillful means, casting reflections throughout the ten directions—this is precisely the intent of "revealing the origin to manifest the fundamental. Regarding the Ten Profundities of Contemplating the Mind:

the single thought-moment before us is fully endowed with the karmic retributions of the ten realms, both good and evil; this is the Profundity of the Object (*viṣaya*). One contemplates this by means of the three types of perfect wisdom.
To investigate this is the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna-miāo*). To cultivate the two contemplations based upon this single reality realm is the excellence of practice (*caryā-miāo*).

To have faith in this mind of one's own, to accord with this mind of one's own, and to realize that this mind of one's own is fundamentally unborn from the beginning is the excellence of the three stages of patience (*kṣānti-miāo*).
To never depart from the secret treasury of one's own mind from beginning to end is the excellence of the three dharmas (*dharma-miāo*). The union of object and wisdom is the response.

It should be wondrous. That wisdom can transform objects is the wondrousness of supernormal power (*abhijñā*). That in a single thought-moment it transforms and teaches other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is the wondrousness of teaching the Dharma.
That other minds and mental factors turn in accordance with its observation is the wondrousness of its retinue. Beginning from the names...

Reaching the ultimate limit is precisely the wondrousness of merit and benefit. Because the Great Being Kṣitigarbha and the Honored One Śākyamuni contemplated the mind, they long ago accomplished the ten wondrousnesses;

their manifested functions are vast and far-reaching. Now, as I contemplate the mind and bring forth these ten wondrousnesses, my manifested functions shall likewise be inexhaustible throughout the bounds of the future. This is the fundamental wondrousness of contemplating the mind. This concludes the specific explanation.
The specific names have concluded. Next, regarding the general name: in Sanskrit it is *sūtra*, or *sūtraka*, or *sūdan*, or *sūtrānta*;
these are merely variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. Some say it has no translation because it contains five meanings;
others say it does have translations: first, it is translated as "Sutra" (Scripture); second, as "Kye" (Agreement/Compact); third, as "Dharmamūla" (Root of Dharma); and fourth, as "Thread" (*sūtra*).

The fifth is the "Wholesome Speech of the Five Turnings," which encompasses five turnings of the five [categories], each possessing the three aspects of teaching (jiao), practice (xing), and principle (li), as detailed in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
This will not be recounted here again. For now, I shall clarify the common and specific aspects based on a single title: "Zhan cha" (Observing and Examining) refers to the teaching.

Wholesome and unwholesome karma are "conduct" (*saṃskāra*). Retribution, which consists of indeterminate form and mind, is the "principle" (*tattva*). Furthermore, "divination" (*jñāna*) is the teaching (*śāsana*), and "examination" (*vicaya*) is conduct;

that wholesome and unwholesome karmic retribution is what is divined and examined constitutes the principle. When these are correlated with the words of the sūtras, they possess both general and specific meanings according to their respective contexts. The explanation of the names is complete.
Second, regarding the manifestation of the essence (*tattva*): the essence is the primary substance; it is that which is signified by a name.
If a sūtra lacked an essence, it would be devoid of the seal of orthodoxy and would be identical to the teachings of Māra.

Therefore, it is necessary to manifest the ultimate aim of this entire section and clarify the convergence of all its meanings. Yet this wondrous essence is not only extremely difficult to realize, but also difficult to explain.
It is unchanging. A sutra states: "The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither empty nor non-empty;
it is devoid of all characteristics and cannot be demonstrated through verbal expression. The Lotus Sutra says: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and their signs are quiescent."
The Great Sūtra states: "Non-arising and non-arising are ineffable. It further states: "Because there are causes and conditions, they can also be spoken of.

This sūtra likewise says that, based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—within the realm of illusory transformations, causes and conditions, and provisional designations (*prajñapti-dharma*)—where things exist in mutual dependence and opposition, they may be skillfully manifested and explained.
Now, I shall briefly set forth seven points. First: Directly manifesting the sūtra.
1. The essence; 2. Distinguishing the false and the spurious; 3. Synonyms for the single dharma; 4. The gateway for entering the essence; 5.
Pervasively serving as the essence of all sutras; 6. Pervasively serving as the essence of all practices; 7. Pervasively serving as the essence of all dharmas.
First, to explicitly reveal the essence of the sutra: it is the single, true realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*).

All realms of the hundred worlds and thousand suchnesses manifest based upon this single, true [nature] through delusion; yet those realms have no separate intrinsic nature of their own, but take only the single truth as their essence.
Therefore, it is called the "single, true realm. One should know that this single truth is the [essence] of all phenomena.

Reality (*tattva*). It is like the moist nature of ice and water. The phenomenal realm (*viṣaya*) is the provisional aspect of all dharmas, just as ice and water are the manifestations of the moist nature.
Although ice and water differ, their moist nature is non-dual; although the phenomenal realms differ, the single reality is without distinction.

Therefore, the single reality of the phenomenal realm is taken as the true essence of the sutra, just as the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the "true aspect of all dharmas" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*). Dharma...
Because the provisional is opened up to reveal the real, all provisional dharmas are gathered and returned to the reality of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This sutra governs the provisional with the real; thus, by citing the reality of the single reality, it subsumes the provisionality of objective realms.
Within the ten realms, it takes only the nature of the retribution for good and evil karma illuminated within the Buddha-realm. This nature is neither born nor extinguished.
Perfectly complete and eternally abiding, it is free from all marks and is identical to all phenomena. Among the ten suchnesses, one takes its essential nature;
among the four conditions, one takes the inconceivable non-arising and non-ceasing; among the twelve links of dependent origination, one takes suffering as the Dharmakāya;
among the fourfold Four Noble Truths, one takes only the truth of non-action; and within that non-action, one takes exclusively the truth of cessation.
Among the seven Two Truths, one takes the latter five True Truths; among the five Three Truths, one takes the Middle Truth in all cases;
among the various One Real Truths, one takes the Perfect One Real Truth; among the various Ineffable Truths, one takes the ineffability of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Among the twenty kinds of wisdom, one takes the Perfect Buddha-wisdom; among the three kinds of patience, one takes the Patience of Non-arising.
Among the four Buddhas, one takes the Buddha of Perfected Meritorious Conduct (*Guṇasampanna*). Among the three virtues, one takes the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should first know the fundamental karma of the initial practice, which is to cultivate faith and understanding by relying upon the single reality realm (*ekasatya-viṣaya*). If there were no single reality realm to serve as a basis, it would be like...
A house has no void; there would be nothing to contain or receive [the objects within]. Therefore, the *Śāstra* says:
"If this emptiness did not exist, everything would have nothing upon which to rely. For this reason, its essence must be revealed.
Second, regarding the elimination of the false and the spurious: this single reality-boundary is not the same as the various worldly dharmas postulated by ordinary people and non-Buddhists;
it is not the same as the events prior to the kalpa of emptiness postulated by those in deviant dhyāna;

it is the supreme point, the countenance prior to the birth of one's parents, beyond even the realm of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranirghoṣa; and it is not the same as the partial truth realized by the Hīnayāna.

This is not the same as the clear, pure *tathatā* explained in the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), nor can it be distinguished merely by relying on the names and designations of the Perfect Teaching (*paryanta-vyavahāra*).
It is only by relying on the two kinds of contemplative paths that one can attain the two types of samādhi: the tranquility of form and the tranquility of mind.
Furthermore, one enters the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi) and abides in firm faith; it is simply a matter of decisive faith and understanding.

Regarding the different names for this single dharma: it is sometimes called the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmasthiti* (dharma-abiding), *dharmapada* (dharma-position), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), *tathatā* (suchness), *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality), *pūrvakoṭi* (original limit), *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (true mark), *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata), *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness), *vijñaptimātratā* (the nature of representation-only), or *svabhāva-viśuddha* (purity of self-nature).
The pure mind; the fundamental source-ground of the mind; the true cause of Buddha-nature; bodhi; nirvāṇa; inconceivable liberation;

the realm of self-realized noble wisdom; the absence of conceptual proliferation; the absence of inversion; the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*); the pure *dharmakāya*;
the great perfect mirror-wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); the central, substantial, and rational mind; the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākāra-jñatā*); and the unshared [qualities].

Prajñā, the Ocean of Perfect and Universal Knowledge, the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Vaipulya, Perfect Enlightenment, Wondrous Enlightenment, Ultimate Enlightenment, and so forth—all these are alternative names for the single reality realm.
They can only be known through the mind; they cannot be fully expressed in words.
Regarding the four gates for entering the essence: the single reality of the objective realm is profound and abstruse, like ascending a precipitous ravine which necessarily requires a flying ladder.
To realize the true source, one must rely upon teaching and practice; therefore, teaching and practice serve as the gates.
If teaching is taken as the gate, there are briefly four types of teaching. Within each teaching, the principle is elucidated by means of four gates, totaling [sixteen].
Regarding the sixteen teaching gates (*ṣoḍaśa-dvāra*), one practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) based on each individual gate. Furthermore, there are sixteen practice gates (*pratipatti-dvāra*).
Attaining awakening through the teachings is called "practice by faith" (*śraddhā-carita*); attaining awakening through contemplation is called "practice by Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).

Whether these function as alternating aspects of teaching and practice or as mutually supportive aspects of teaching and practice, they will not be discussed in detail here. The four gates of the Tripitaka teachings all converge upon the single reality (*eka-tattva*). Far...

Furthermore, they are clumsy and must await further revelation. The four gates of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) lead to the One Reality; though skillful, they remain distant and thus require transition.
The four gates of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) lead to the One Reality; though proximate, they are clumsy.

Only the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) truly lead to the One Reality, for these alone are skillful and direct. The characteristics of the four gates in each of the three preceding teachings are likewise as follows:
Setting aside further elaboration, to briefly clarify the characteristics of the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): one gate is all gates, and all gates are one gate.
It is neither one nor four, yet we speak of four and one. As the Sūtra says: "Within the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata..."

Although it is beyond the realm of verbal expression, free from mental conceptions and recollections, neither empty nor non-empty, and even devoid of all characteristics such that it cannot be indicated by words, it can nevertheless be demonstrated through skillful means.
For the nature of that Dharmakāya is truly without discrimination; it is free from self-characteristics and free from other-characteristics, being neither empty nor non-empty.
Because one has distanced oneself from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), that essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is said to be ultimately empty and non-existent.
Since mental discrimination and conceptualization have ceased, there is not a single mark that can be seen or known by itself as existing.
Therefore, the meaning of emptiness is definitively true, corresponding to reality without error; this is precisely the emptiness of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).
Regarding the characteristics of the gates: emptiness is identical to the other three; they do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, it is said that within the meaning of that very emptiness, because one is free from the conceptualizing and deluded thoughts of the mind, there is ultimately not a single characteristic that can be called empty.
Because only the ultimate reality exists, it is "not empty. This is what is meant by being free from the perceptions of consciousness; there is nothing [else].
All marks of falsity are ultimately eternal, constant, unchanging, and undifferentiated, for there is not a single mark further to be destroyed or extinguished,
as they are free from increase or decrease. Furthermore, in that state of non-conceptual reality, from beginningless time,
it has been endowed with immeasurable meritorious qualities and natural activities, which are perfectly accomplished and correspondingly present, never being separate from one another.
Because it is liberated [from these], it is said to be "not empty. This is precisely the aspect of the "Gate of Existence" (*yu-mén*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).
"Existence" here refers to the other three [aspects], which do not contradict one another. Furthermore, it says:

Although all sentient beings possess this mass of real essence and merit, because they are shrouded and obstructed by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), they neither know nor see it, and are unable to realize or attain its function.
Virtue and benefit are no different from non-existence; they are described as "not yet being.

This is precisely the characteristic of the gate of both existence and emptiness in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which does not contradict the other three gates. Furthermore, it is said: "All dharmas do not depart from the essence of Bodhi.
The essence of Bodhi is neither existent nor non-existent. Even if there should be conceptual discrimination," and so forth.

This would then be false and deceptive, and cannot be called "correspondence. This is precisely the characteristic of the "neither existence nor emptiness" gate of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which does not contradict the other three gates.
To briefly indicate the contemplation for entering the gateway of Dharma practice:

the characteristics of the four gates as previously described are themselves the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Those of superior faculties can realize and enter this realm through their contemplation. As...
If one has not yet awakened, one should rely upon this object and again resolve upon the Great Bodhicitta: "Such a wondrous realm—the Buddhas and sentient beings—are equal to me.
Why is it that while the Buddhas have already awakened, I and all sentient beings remain deluded and unaware, unable to enjoy it?
With such sorrowful lamentation, one establishes the Four Great Vows; thus, one may awaken and enter [the path]. If, as before...
If you have not yet awakened, diligently practice and study with faith in the contemplation of the mind through *śamatha* and with faith in the contemplation of the mind through *vipaśyanā*;

then you will be able to awaken and enter [the truth] suddenly and expansively. If you still have not awakened, continue to use the contemplation of mind-only consciousness to break down all phenomena as being emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Through true suchness-contemplation (*tathatā-bhūta-vedanā*), do not dwell upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and forever leave behind the notion of "one."
One should then awaken to and enter [this state]. If one has not yet awakened, one should personally examine each section of the body to discern what is obstructed and what is unobstructed;
by relying on that Great Being’s skillful exposition of the profound Dharma, one shall abandon timidity and weakness, and will certainly be able to awaken and enter.

If one has still not awakened, one should diligently cultivate the two contemplations, observing the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, so as to realize that form and mind are fundamentally quiescent.

This is precisely the perfection of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). From this, through the appropriate application of right effort, the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), one enters the perfection of the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). This is the characteristic of those with middling faculties entering the Path.
If you have still not attained realization, you should at all times and in all places constantly and diligently recite the name of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha. You should contemplate the earth...
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata and the Dharmakāyas of all Buddhas are equal in essence to one's own body;
they are non-dual and undifferentiated, unborn and unceasing, eternal, blissful, self, and pure, with perfected virtues—thus they are worthy of refuge.

Furthermore, one should observe the characteristics of one's own body and mind as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; they are like illusions and transformations, and thus should be viewed with revulsion and detachment.
Even the methods for practicing repentance shown in the preceding fascicle are all skillful means that serve as antidotes to facilitate awakening.
Moreover, a sutra states: "If a person has not yet attained the auspicious signs of the three karmas, or if they see light..."
If one perceives the scent of extraordinary fragrances or dreams of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emitting light as a sign of realization, these are merely false, delusive, and deceptive.

Furthermore, the explanations regarding the distinctions between the three types of patience (*kṣānti*) and the four Buddhas are all intended to enable the practitioner to clearly recognize the successive stages and avoid the arising of overweening pride (*abhimāna*). Moreover, one must not [cling to] such false, delusive, and deceptive signs.

To take up and cling [to them] is precisely patience (*kṣānti*). Not delighting in the various worldly dhyānas and samādhis, nor likewise delighting in the two vehicles (*yāna*), is precisely the departure from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

To carefully examine the scriptural text, although the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) and the fulfillment of the meaning (*artha-pūrṇa*) do not follow a sequential order, they may fortunately serve as proof.
One should know that apart from the ten vehicle methods, there is no other gateway for entering contemplation.
Regarding the five aspects that constitute the essence of all sutras: this single reality-realm is what is collectively elucidated by thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises.
Without this, the *Avataṃsaka* would have no means to manifest the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
Without this, the *Āgamas* would have no means to manifest quiescent nirvana. Without this, the *Vaipulya* sutras would have no means to manifest the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Dharma-gates: were it not for Prajñā, there would be no means to manifest the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Were it not for the Lotus Sūtra, there would be no means to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the true reality (*tattva*) of the One Vehicle.

Were it not for the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, there would be no means to manifest the eternal Buddha-nature and the secret treasury of the three virtues. Therefore, throughout the teachings of the one lifetime—whether partial or complete—[it is through these that the ultimate truth is revealed].
Whether provisional or real, they ultimately all take the single true realm as their essence; they ultimately all merely point back to and take refuge in the single true realm.
Regarding the six aspects being the essence of all practices, there are further three meanings. First, a general discussion of the sixteen [aspects] across the four teachings.
Each gate has two types of practice—those based on faith and those based on the Dharma—all of which are accomplished by relying upon the single reality of the objective realm.
Second, when discussing the establishment of practices according to the sutras individually, they do not exceed four kinds: namely, the constantly walking samādhi and the constantly sitting samādhi.
The Samādhi of Half-Walking and Half-Sitting, and the Samādhi of Neither-Walking-nor-Sitting. These also take the one true realm as their essence and can be known through the mind.
Regarding the present sutra, there are further two parts. First, the method of repentance is clarified:
following the offerings, prostrations, confession of sins, entreaties, sympathetic joy, and dedication of merit, one may either sit upright and recite...
Whether reciting while walking or circumambulating, this is subsumed under the *svacittāśaya-samādhi* (the samādhi that follows one's own intent), which is neither walking nor sitting.

Second, to specifically clarify the two contemplations: at all times and in all places, whatever actions are performed by means of body, speech, and mind, one should always observe and know them to be nothing but mind, and so forth; thus, one may practice by traversing the twelve links of dependent origination.

One practices two types of contemplation, which are not restricted to either walking or sitting. These two paths of contemplation are correctly based upon the single reality realm (*ekasatya-dhātu*) to cultivate faith and understanding;
apart from this, there is no separate essence of practice. This need not be further explained.

May all sentient beings swiftly reach the source of the mind and forever extinguish the roots of transgression.

Furthermore, the third wheel-mark states: "All such numbers arise from the number one;

It arises from the single reality realm of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).
Taking this single reality realm as its basis, is it not the case that the Dharma of the three types of wheel-signs is demonstrated by relying upon this single reality realm?
If one cannot know the single reality realm, then all conditioned practices (*saṃskāra*) are rendered in vain. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If [the mind] is confused and distracted..."
With a defiled mind, even though one recites my name, it cannot be called "hearing" [the Dharma], because one is unable to give rise to resolute faith and understanding.
One merely obtains worldly rewards of merit and fails to attain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits.
Thus, with such a distracted and defiled mind, all the various virtues one cultivates will fail to yield deep and great results.
Benefit. You should know that all those who have not yet understood the realm of the single reality are said to possess a confused and defiled mind.
If one can understand and realize the realm of the single reality, then there is only this single reality and no other realms; therefore, there is no confusion.
Because its self-nature is pure, there is no defilement. From the absence of confusion and defilement regarding names and designations, up to the ultimate absence thereof—
The defilements of confusion all proceed based upon the single reality-basis; therefore, it is specifically the essence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Seventh, regarding its being the essence of all dharmas universally: the Sūtra says, "Because they rely upon the single reality-basis, there is that [existence] and non-existence."
[The text] clarifies: failing to understand the single dharma-realm, one erroneously applies thought and reflection, whereby false objects manifest.

○ Third, clarifying the school (zong): although the essence was manifested previously, it was merely the principle-nature (li-xing). This principle-nature is equal and all-encompassing.
Birth is co-existent [with the body]. Although one may point to ice and say it is water, and no longer seek it elsewhere, if one wishes to drink it, it must still be melted.
Furthermore, although space exists, one must have beams, pillars, and rafters to support a house before it can be used;
if this house lacks its structural framework, it will ultimately be ravaged by wind, sun, rain, and dew. So it is for all sentient beings.

To suffer various afflictions while being deluded regarding the emptiness of the *dharmatā* is likewise so. Therefore, after revealing the essence (*tī*), one must immediately clarify the fundamental principle (*zōng*).
The fundamental principle is the guiding framework for practice and the urgent task for realizing the essence. When the main rope is lifted, all the tassels are drawn together;
when the collar is grasped, the sleeves and lapels follow in full. It is like hot water dissolving ice; such is the nature of *dharmatā*.
Water thus appears. Just as when the rafters are completed, the chamber of the secret treasury becomes habitable, so too does this sutra take two kinds of contemplative paths as its primary doctrine:
first, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness; second, the contemplation of true suchness (tathatā). Regarding the contemplation of mind-only consciousness:

it is the knowledge that there are only deluded thoughts and no real objective realm, and that these thoughts themselves are subject to arising and ceasing, abiding for not even a moment. From this...
One shall attain the Samādhi of the Quiescence of Form. Regarding the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness), one contemplates that the nature of the mind is neither arising nor ceasing;

Now, the realm of the single reality is neither form nor mind; it is only because of ignorance and lack of understanding that it falsely becomes dualistic.
The Dharma is like pressing upon the eye and falsely seeing two moons. Based on the deluded mind, one discriminates deluded forms; due to deluded forms, the deluded mind is revealed.
Thus, the mind serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for form, and form also serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind.
If one knows that form is merely a manifestation of the mind and that there is no form external to the mind, this is called the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
One can attain the samādhi of the stillness of form; when form is still, the mind is also still.
If one knows that the mind has only a name and is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, this is the true contemplation of suchness, by which one can attain the samādhi of the stillness of mind;

To give rise to the mind of profound and vast practice and abide in the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*) constitutes "Buddha-as-such-like" (*pratibimba-buddhatva*).

○ Fifth, regarding the classification of the teachings (*śāsanalakṣaṇa*): this is subsumed within the Mahayana Vaipulya teachings. It guides those of the three capacities (*trividha-indriya*) to return to the single reality (*ekasatya*).
Furthermore, it enables even those who lack the resolve to seek the essential path to be liberated from all decline and affliction, and to be born in [the Pure Land].
This is the "Expedient Means" (Upāya). Indeed, there is no dharma not fully contained herein, and no capacity that is not accommodated.

This means that while it also encompasses all classes of beings with gradual capacities, its primary intent lies solely in the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun) teaching. The section on the characteristics of the teachings concludes.
